When solving large-scale linear systems arising from the discretization of partial differential equations, iterative methods such as GMRES or MINRES are commonly utilized. These algorithms benefit significantly from the inherent structure of these systems, particularly their symmetry in the case of MINRES, when applied. However, this advantage is often compromised due to the loss of matrix structure resulting from numerical integration and spatial discretization. This work proposes a novel approach to preserve the essential zero-block patterns, crucial for system sparsity, by utilizing efficient sparse preconditioners. These tools aim to restore the inherent matrix symmetries, thereby enhancing the performance of iterative solvers in this context.

We developed a novel approach for matching 3D dental models to a standardized upper jaw template, taking into account the complex, asymmetric nature of jaw movements. Our method models the jaw's asymmetrical behavior using a biomechanical approach, accounting for joint displacement and rigid-body movement. By incorporating mass-spring systems, our algorithm efficiently matches point clouds to a template with two stages of optimization. Experimental results show our approach can accurately match low-res jaw volume data with a high degree of precision and recall. We also demonstrate our method's capability to align high-fresh CT-based jaw models.

This paper introduces two novel metrics, Frobenius norm and singular value decomposition, for evaluating the accuracy of scene flow estimates in the presence of distorted metric spaces. It considers two primary challenges in deep learning-based flow estimation: pixel-wise and location-aware errors. To tackle these challenges, the proposed methods go beyond traditional approaches by decomposing flow fields into foreground and background components and incorporating human-interpretable loss functions. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of these methods, achieving superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques on the KITTI and SUTOMO datasets.

In recent years, Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have excelled in various classification tasks. However, their high computational demands lead to slow inference speeds and substantial energy consumption. In contrast, Spiking Neural Network (SNN) classifiers offer low-latency operations and efficient energy usage. To combine the best of both worlds, we have integrated the two technologies to create a robust and adaptable method for data annotation. We propose a novel hybrid approach that leverages the efficiency of SNNs and the performance of DNNs for accurate and sustainable data labeling.

This research investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of a spin-aligned strange quark star in the presence of a strong magnetic field at high temperatures. A novel model has been developed to describe the equation of state for these stars, combining the Maxwell's formalism to handle the transition between hadronic and quark phases within a strong magnetic field. The effects of temperature, quark mass, and the magnetic field on the structure of these stars have been analyzed by solving the modified Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations. According to our findings, an increase in temperature can lead to a transformation from a hadronic star to a strange quark star, and then back to a hadronic star at extremely high temperatures; an increase in the magnetic field strength results in a compression of the stellar structure; and in the presence of a strong magnetic field, axial chemical potential stars exhibit unlike behavior compared to their aligned counterparts.

This research paper introduces the concepts of ideal matchings and ideal coverings within the framework of cubic graphs. Building upon the definition of a matching and a cover, these new notions were defined by H. K. Truong, a former student of A. I. S. Newell. It has been proven that every cubic graph contains at least one ideal matching and every cubic graph's edges can be covered by at least one ideal covering. Additionally, a matching is defined as perfect when its size equals that of the graph's vertex set, and an cover is minimal when its size equals that of the graph's edge set. Furthermore, this study combines the notions of ideal matchings and minimal coverings to define the idea of an ideal tinting of a cubic graph.

To enhance the performance of networked systems, various techniques have been employed through specialized hardware and software methodologies. Historically, reinforcement learning has been successfully applied to clarify and rectify AS call handling procedures. However, the efficacy of these approaches relies heavily on access to comprehensive packet data, which limits their widespread adoption due to privacy concerns. A novel framework called Timeloops is presented that enables the investigation of containerized microservice systems from an end-to-end perspective, allowing for performance optimization without compromising data accessibility. This framework is demonstrated through an actual AS call handling scenario, yielding a 20 percent container drop rate reduction, equivalent to improved system reliability.

This study develops a new birth model for multi-object filtering that combines the advantages of parametric and grid-based models. By representing the objects' intensity as a sum of Dirac masses, the proposed model leverages the efficiency of Kalman filtering for known parameter objects and a PDA filter for unknown objects. A novel mixed filter is then introduced to combine these individual filters while accounting for the objects' unknown positions. The result is a optimized solution that applies the linearized Cardinality Probability Hypothesis Density filter with a partial grid, and two alternative versions of this filter are also introduced. The filter's efficiency is demonstrated in the context of sensor administration.

This study examines the null controllability of a competitive system in a one-dimensional domain that features community dynamics and an order-zero degeneration in its competitive interactions within the interior of the domain's space. It is demonstrated that steering at least part of the population towards a predefined state can be achieved without any cost growth as the intensity of interior competition increases without limit.

By examining soccer matches, we focus on analyzing their dynamics through state, action, and reward spaces, with the goal of formulating strategies to score goals. A critical aspect of this research involves developing and testing two different soccer situations where points are scarce, specifically with one team leading 1-0 with three minutes remaining, or trailing 2-0 with eight minutes left. A third scenario is also considered, where a team is ahead 3-0 with fifteen minutes to go. Through these examples, we demonstrate the feasibility of using reinforcement learning to navigate complex real-world problems in soccer. A key contribution of this study is identifying key learning patterns when a team is behind in a soccer game. However, due to the high stochasticity of these situations, reinforcement learning proves limited in its effectiveness in significantly reducing errors in decision-making. Consequently, we propose more reliable methods for generating optimal behavior in these critical moments.

Wave equation-based inverse modeling has seen significant progress, particularly in subsurface surface waveform inversion (FWI), which has achieved high-resolution subsurface models. FWI's reliance on accurate simulated wavefields for data-driven misfit calculations presents a challenge, as wavefield accuracy is constrained by approximations and sampling limitations. These constraints can lead to inaccurate FWI results. To address this issue, it is crucial to incorporate a substituted wavefield with higher fidelity, such as a time-domain amplified source (TAS) signal. TAS signals can be used to calculate a higher-fidelity wavefield by solving a regularization-posed amplified source equation, yielding a TAS impulse response that maintains its amplification properties while preserving the original source signal's key features. This response can be applied to calculate a higher-fidelity wavefield without losing accuracy or introducing phase shifts, and without increasing memory usage significantly. Furthermore, TAS signals and corresponding simulated wavefields can be efficiently calculated using second-order accuracy finite-difference methods, allowing for a cost-effective improvement in subsurface imaging.

To model how two competing species interact and decide on coexistence or the elimination of one, a chaotic version of the voter model has been developed, taking into consideration their dispersal rates. This model incorporates a colonization competition tradeoff into a model previously developed by Balasubramanian and Holmes. Our study uses dynamical systems theory and numerical simulations to analyze the model and find that a set of complex attractors can emerge, including what is known as a strange attractor, holding multiple unstable limit cycles. We find that the model indicates that the extinction of one species is an inevitable outcome in certain tradeoff scenarios, whereas different regions of parameter space offer conditions where the species can coexist stably or oscillate in numbers. Ultimately, the model demonstrates that external influences can lead to complex dynamics, non-monotonic relationships between the competition intensity and the population of one species, and that intermediate levels of external influence offer the best chance for coexistence.

This research focuses on an innovative integrated information and energy (IIE) network that incorporates D2D communication. This network is unusual because it utilizes an intellect reflecting surface (IRS) element. This special component allows the network to not only transfer data but also generate power. To accomplish this, part of the IRS element uses active circuitry powered by harvested energy to modify the phase and amplitude of signals. To effectively allocate resources and distribute computational tasks across this network, we developed a new algorithm based on an intelligent backtracking method. This algorithm AND an optimal star graph theory are key components of our integrated approach. To further test the reliability of our results, we also utilized a genetic algorithm (GA). Our findings demonstrate that our new integrated approach is effective in managing resources and distributing computational tasks across this unusual IIE D2D network.

A laser Doppler velocimeter is an instrument used to quickly and highly accurately
measure the velocity of objects. In typical use, the operator must stand in the
path of the laser's safety corridor to input new coordinates into the system,
which can be time-consuming and uncomfortable for participants, especially when
conducting large-scale measurements on extensive surfaces. To address this
limitation, this project develops a method for remotely controlling an single-point
laser Doppler velocimeter to broaden its usable range. By integrating the velocimeter
with a freely movable two-dimensional surface, this approach allows for faster
and more comfortable data collection, enabling the efficient acquisition of
large datasets. The successful implementation of this method is demonstrated
through the collection of 3 velocity component fields in three different scenarios,
each comprising approximately 15,000 data points, within a region of 1.2 meters by
1.2 meters.

The effectiveness of programmable phase discs (PPDs) is being analyzed as potential correctors for spherical and chromatic aberrations in electron microscopes (TEMs). Both traditional phase discs and PPDs are compared using pen-and-paper calculations, Monte Carlo simulations, and experimental data obtained from an actual TEM with spherical chromatic aberrations. The results show that while a PPD can compensate for these imaging defects, the random drift of electrons causes the focal length to change, leading to significant damage being depicted in high-resolution images. The research also considers the potential of PPDs to be used at the sample stage in an scanning TEM and concludes that their success relies on minimizing the electron drift or using a non-volatile memory. The research aims to provide a framework for evaluating the potential of using a range of spatially and temporally variable magnetic multipole elements at various stages in an electron microscope.

We investigate the spectral and orbital stability of small amplitude solutions to the Klein-Gordon equation with an anharmonic oscillator. Our analysis shows that the linearized equation possesses no embedded eigenvalues within the continuous spectrum band. Furthermore, under a specific condition, we prove the absence of any discrete eigenvalues in the same band, thereby confirming a conjecture previously proposed by Disconatin, Holmer, and Smirnov.

We derive new outcomes regarding quadratic separators $Q(\mathfrak{n})$ of numbers $n$ within specific ideal classes of an imaginary quadratic field $K$. These outcomes depend on the properties of the non-commutative ring $\mathcal{O}_K[\mathfrak{n}]$. If this ring lacks a Leibmer constant for the extender $V_{\mathfrak{n}}$ of the field $K$, we prove that most quadratic separators lie in a single order of magnitude. If this ring has a Leibmer constant for the extender $V_{\mathfrak{n}}$ of the intender $\mathfrak{n}_0$ of the monoid $[\mathfrak{n}]$, we establish that the count of primitive Heilbronn triples residing in a specific range is directly related to the two dimensions. We also provide an algorithm to identify conditions under which this ring possesses the property of the non-commutative class number formula. These theoretical advances build on the work of various researchers including Cauchermann, Lackaby, Le Boudec, and others.

In experiments involving particle collisions, identifying invisible or indirectly detected decay products poses a significant challenge, particularly when they result from alternative physics processes. To address this challenge, we have developed an algorithm capable of identifying alternative decay channels of $B$ mesons, either emitting axion-like particles through the process $B^0\to X_X_X$ or occurring without any detectable output as $B^0\to \emptyset$. This method allows for the efficient search for new physics within the datasets collected by Belle II. If axion-like particles were discovered, they would offer invaluable information about the underlying particle physics and provide a distinctive signal that could be differentiated from other alternative decay processes as the data collected by future particle accelerators becomes increasingly detailed. If Belle II were to find no evidence of axion-like particles, it would allow for more precise limits to be set on their production, again providing an improved constraint compared to previous experiments collected by previous particle accelerators. Consequently, if Belle II were to collect 50 million electron-positron pairs, it would allow for several hundred thousand opportunities to detect specific alternative decay channels of $B$ mesons as they occur, including $B^0\to \gamma_X$, $B^0\to e^+\gamma_X$, and $B^0\to \gamma_X_X$, or set precise limits on their occurrence rates.

This work investigates semantic shifts in word meanings using contextualized language representations. We examined high-dimensional vector spaces from BERT and GLoVe models, employing techniques to analyze contextual representations and extracted local structures. Our analysis reveals that contextual models effectively capture historical shifts in word semantics, particularly anomalous changes. We developed three hypotheses - the Projection Hypothesis, Modality Hypothesis, and Hybrid Hypothesis - to explain how contextual representations encode linguistic semantics. Additionally, we found that contextual models possess an intrinsic geometric property, allowing for the extraction of local contextual relationships through various projections. Our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of contextualized language representations and their temporal dynamics, highlighting the utility of geometric analysis in interpreting these representations.

When matter falls on supermassive black holes, their accretion disks can cause the black hole's event horizon and the surrounding spacetime to rotate, which in turn affects the spectral lines that result from the movement of ionized gas. By analyzing historical spectroscopic data, researchers were able to use this phenomenon of superradiance to assess the potential for spacetime frame-dragging and, consequently, for testing theories of general relativity and the behavior of ultralight particles. To do this, they created a method for accounting for the impact of frame-rotation effects on observed orbital velocities and then applied it to a sample of 43 emission-line spectra from the SDSS-MAGCAT catalog. They found spacetime frame-rotation effects to be significant and non-negligible for all the observed objects, which allowed them to test the effects of ultralight bosons and determine their mass range. They also developed an improved model for describing rotating gas disks that could be used in similar studies in the future.

A distinctive characteristic of neuroblast development is the migration of nuclei across the retinal surface during the interphase, a behavior known as retinal interkinetic nuclear migration (IKNM). This study investigates zebrafish retina dynamics using a combination of mathematical modeling and advanced imaging techniques, revealing that the observed Z-stack oscillations of nuclei result from a diffusive process with distinct in-phase and out-of-phase diffusive components. Our findings suggest that an initially non-diffusive IKNM model can be made to exhibit diffusion-based behavior through the application of multiplicative gating functions. Furthermore, we propose that an active cell intrinsic "timer" mechanism, previously hypothesized to drive IKNM, may be unnecessary, as diffusion-based models accurately replicate the observed dynamics of zebrafish retinal nuclei.

In a recent study, we investigate the challenges of implementing code-based source isolation in compressive video retrieval. We specifically examine the source isolation technique developed by Yu et al. (2022), and identify limitations in their current framework. We believe two main areas require further investigation: first, utilizing color images to distinguish sources requires an effective error correcting code, and second, isolating sources in compressive video data is complicated by time-varying code mappings. We propose a novel approach to address the first issue, and investigate the second using a combination of code mapping estimation and reordering techniques. We believe our findings contribute valuable insights and practical solutions to improving source isolation in compressive video retrieval.

This paper formulates and analyzes the polar Navier-Stokes equations in an environment with disordered obstacles that are impermeable, denoted as $\obst$, within $d$-dimensional space, where the number of dimensions is greater than two. The coefficients of these equations are influenced by the configuration of the disordered environment. Initially, the model was applied to describe the behavior of complex fluids in two dimensions by Forster, Robinson, and Swift in 1977, and subsequently used to simulate liquid helium in its specific thermal state in three dimensions by Hohenberg and Swift in 1977 or 1978. The primary objective of our investigation is to establish the short-term existence and uniqueness of weak solutions to these equations. To achieve this result, we do not require the boundaries of the disordered obstacles to be smooth; they can be irregular. Moreover, we can even handle the case where the obstacles are of different shapes and orientations. To prove our main finding, we rely on the technique of compactness derived from the arguments initially proposed by Panagiotopoulos and Cess in 1974, augmented with our own innovations.

Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology has experienced significant growth over the last few years, particularly in high-density language contexts such as Indonesian. Although OCR has been highly effective in low-density languages, it struggles with accuracy in Indonesian due to the complex structure and grammatical rules of the language. This research aims to enhance the accuracy of an existing Indonesian ID document extraction system by utilizing a Natural Language approach to parse extracted text from an ID card. The system was tested using 500 datasets, revealing that the proposed method successfully extracted first name, middle name, and last name components with a high level of accuracy, allowing for the system's performance to be reliably estimated.

We examine the quantum harmonic oscillator with a driving force by employing the path integral formulation. Without relying on Heisenberg equations of motion, we derive an analytical solution to the path integral for a driven harmonic oscillator. Then, we utilize the Metropolis-Hastings and Hybrid Monte Carlo methods to compute the propagator for this system, validating our results through analytical findings. Ultimately, these methods facilitate direct comparison and validation of our classical trajectory calculations with the propagator outcomes.

The YORP effect causes small asteroids to accelerate their rotation at varying rates. Researchers discovered that the YORP effect has a more significant impact on certain asteroids than others, which can lead to fragmentation, surface changes, and complete destruction as they approach the end of their lives. Although some characteristics can be directly attributed to YORP-induced effects, many aspects remain unclear or speculative. In order to better understand the YORP effect's manifestations on asteroids, this study focuses on three specific examples: (10115) 1992 SK, (1685) Toro, and (1620) Geographos, for which shape models, surface features, and light curves are available. By analyzing the YORP-induced changes in these asteroids' rotation speeds, this study estimates their mass densities and compares them to similar asteroids. Furthermore, this study categorizes the YORP effect's impact on these asteroids based on their shape, composition, and the intensity of solar radiation they experience, which allows for a better prediction of their future behavior.
We show that any subgroup of F^+(M) which is not compact when viewed as a subgroup of Homeo_(c)(M) is not Roelcke precompact as a subgroup of Homeo(M).

We analyze the operational capabilities of infinite string automata under a broad category of computable transformations. Specifically, we investigate which types of Cauchy-name recognizing automata can define the image of a given set of infinite sequences when subjected to various operations like shuffling, commutation, deletion, S-box application, subsequence extraction, and Brickhouse extraction, across both finite and non-finite collections of references. Furthermore, we employ Parigot's degree model to characterize the computability implications of these extraction-based commutations for infinite strings.

A primary way animals gather food is through foraging. In some cases, foraging herds feed on scattered resources, while in other denser settings, they may graze on more uniformly distributed vegetation. We focus on a specific type of herbivore known as a puller, which removes vegetation and creates gaps in the landscape, then works cooperatively to move these openings to new areas to sustain a high density of food. Although pull-based coexistence lets these animals thrive, it demands careful coordination within the group. Here we develop and analyze a model that accounts for the collective movement of pullers with varying levels of internal competition for leadership roles. Our findings reveal that highly competitive puller societies can successfully maintain food supplies through their level of cooperation, but excessive competition hampers this capability. However, for less social species, pull-based coexistence remains feasible provided there's some degree of spatial separation. These results offer a biological framework where pull-based foraging could flourish, potentially offering an explanatory hypothesis for a observed phenomenon in the behavior of giant pandas.

In control theory and differential games, the focus is on differential Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equations, which can be complex due to the non-differentiability of the viscosity solution in certain scenarios, hindering the development of practical control laws and strategies. This study introduces a novel approach, the Computation of Achievable Sets, which represents an extension of controllability analysis, and demonstrates that, for a differential Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation, second-order information about reachable regions can be obtained, provided sufficient regularity conditions are met. This method also holds validity within differential games, enabling the determination of defendable areas within a differential Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation.

The human ventral temporal cortex, located on the side of the head, is where meaningful representations of social figures such as humans and animals are thought to reside. However, what exactly constitutes this 'animacy' representation and its fundamental nature remain topics of debate within the scientific community. Some researchers believe that this concept is simply a combination of 'species-specific' knowledge, asserting that the animacy signal can be accurately predicted based on previously known patterns in the ventral temporal cortex. In contrast, we argue that the animacy signal is more complex and cannot be reduced to a combination of 'species-specific' components. Instead, it exhibits essential independence and provides valuable predictive power in revealing the neural foundations of our understanding of animals in the region. Furthermore, we found that this representational structure is intimately connected to another distinct dimension of 'inanimacy', demonstrated by inanimate entities such as living organisms and man-made things, demonstrating that the animacy dimension serves as the core of the ventral temporal cortex's complex web of associations.

This research extends our previous findings about the efficient quantum unique ergodicity phenomenon. For any Dirichlet character $\chi \neq \bar{1}$, we show that as the conductor $q$ of $\chi$ approaches 1, the associated $L$-function $L(s,\chi)` has equivalent average behavior to that of newforms with respect to their COE-normalized functional equations, under the condition that $q$ is within a certain range relative to the weight $k$. This equivalence in quantum unique ergodicity and level asymptotics matches the efficiency of a well-known relation derived by Duke, Friedland, and Iwaniec. However, it also stands in contrast to what happens with trivial character, where equivalence emerges only at a much higher cost in terms of level asymptotics, exceeding the bounds established by Chebotarov and Zhang.

We have developed Quantum Relational Hoare Calculus with Expectations, a novel framework that extends traditional relational Hoare logic for verifying pairwise properties of dual algorithms, by incorporating dual invariants and expectations, and by defining correctness as non-decreasing behavior. This framework enables efficient proof of non-strict improvement, which is crucial for ensuring that one algorithm outperforms its counterpart, by leveraging dual invariants and expectations. We demonstrated the practical application of this framework with an example involving non-trivial performance improvement. Moreover, we have shown how quantum protocols, such as the BB84 protocol, can be verified using this framework.

Recent studies emphasize the significant influence of "super-spreader" events on the rapid transmission of infectious diseases, particularly in their early stages. To investigate the effects of these events, we developed an SIR model, incorporating both stochastic and deterministic models with and without the presence of super-spreader incidents. Our results show that such events can significantly affect the epidemic's course in its initial stages, leading to a sudden and substantial rise in new infections, as observed in real-world data, such as the COVID-19 case in Italy, where a large number of cases were concentrated in a single event in North Italy, occurring alongside similar occurrences in other regions of the country at the same time. Furthermore, we found that delaying medical intervention following a super-spreader incident could lead to an increased total number of infected individuals, whereas prompt implementation of containment measures could reduce the total number of cases, especially in populations with a high level of susceptibility to infection. In addition to a populace that is highly susceptible, we discovered that variations in self-protection behaviors and social isolation practices had a substantial effect on the number of new infections resulting from a super-spreader incident. Our research also examined a population divided into two groups, one with high susceptibility and another with low susceptibility, showing that the location and target population of a super-spreader incident could significantly affect the epidemic's course. Our findings highlight the need to monitor and analyze super-spreader events, as they play a crucial role in the rapid transmission of infectious diseases.

Let's consider a topological vector space, denoted as X, and a collection of operators, labeled ω, acting on X. The concept of codiskcyclicity is explored in this study, specifically the codiskcyclicity of an individual operator, a set of operators, and a particular configuration known as the codiskcyclic shift. The codiskcyclicity of the shift operator is proven to be equivalent to the cocyclicity of the associated collection ω, which is further broken down into more manageable conditions outlined in Theorem 3.3. The theoretical framework is then applied to examine the codiskcyclicity of the shift in abstract (semi-)normed spaces of measurable functions, including Lebesgue spaces Lp(φ).

The primary goal of this research was to identify and address potential sources of bias in the estimated vector magnetic field measurements, particularly in the B_T component. This study examined several estimation methods, including minimum entropy rates (MER), unweighted and weighted least squares (LS), and non-negative matrix factorization (NMF). By analyzing synthetic data with known inputs and actual solar data from the HMI instrument, we found that MER often leads to the underestimation of small magnetic features, whereas LS and NMF can result in their overestimation, all of which contribute to the formation of bias in inferred measurements, especially the B_T component. Additionally, this study explored various approaches to reduce this bias, including combining different estimation methods and adjusting pixel-based NMF constraints, which we evaluated using a proxy known as the residuals of fit (ReF).

Simulating quantum systems filled with fermionic particles through Monte Carlo simulations faces a significant challenge known as the hubbard sign dilemma, which can impede simulation accuracy. A recent study proposes employing complex-valued neural networks to overcome this dilemma in the context of the two-dimensional hubbard model. These networks are trained to maintain a near-linear connection between simulation weights and fermionic particle configurations, effectively reducing variance. This study finds that various complex network structures can be utilized to achieve this goal, with the most successful ones demonstrating a simple, partially complex connection. Furthermore, these networks excel not only in moderate conditions but also in highly frustrated scenarios, with sources of remaining complex components being revealed. A particularly straightforward network design is also found to outperform all other designs across a wide range of scenarios.

Given any non-trivial free monoid homomorphism that acts on letters, we've discovered that both topological and factor sequence complexities decrease, unless the output language is finitely recognizable, in which case these parameters are finite. We've also established its stability under certain injective free monoid homomorphisms that can be reversed. Furthermore, any such homomorphism's impact on topological entropy is quantifiable, based on the complexities of the input and output alphabets and the size of a specific matrix associated with the homomorphism. Our study has letters-altering a free monoid's relations as a particular application.

In our work, we've explored how unsupervised task knowledge can enhance natural language processing models when faced with new tasks. Through novel experiments combining question answering and textual entailment tasks, we've created an approach that utilizes unsupervised general knowledge to enhance entailment models through retrieval-based mechanisms. This allows us to formulate the cross-task generalization problem and investigate the effectiveness of unsupervised entailment generalization when moving to a related, but distinct, textual entailment domain. Further analysis of our results enables us to pinpoint the most effective components, analyze the exchangeability of labels, and establish the existence of unsupervised few-shot and zero-shot generalization capabilities. All code and data are publicly accessible for examination.

This work investigates the hyperparameter tuning process for deeply privatized machine learning models in the context of multi-round optimization. We examine the sensitivity of private deep learning models' evaluation metrics to various hypotheses and propose using the privately robust gradient projection (PRGP) algorithm to minimize this sensitivity. Experimental results based on the CIFAR10 and CelebA datasets demonstrate that meticulously tuning critical hyperparameters, particularly the learning rate, is essential for successfully applying deep learning with deep privacy preservation. Our findings highlight that learning rate values determined through meticulous adjustment significantly outperform those tested randomly. Furthermore, we discovered that publicly released deep learning code is highly susceptible to counteracts effects of deep privacy preservation, emphasizing the importance of openly sharing such models while safeguarding individual data.

This study focus on I(n), which represents the lattice of substructures for pairs (f,g) within M_n under a specific ordering relation. A particular substructure is highlighted, denoted as J(I(n)), analogous to Jensen's lattice. It is demonstrated that J(I(n)) is distributive for n=4, yet not semimodular, and is neither semimodular nor distributive for values of n ranging from 5 to 7, and for any n≥8. A comparison is also made of the number of atoms in J(I(n)) with the number of atoms in I(n).

We developed a novel approach, termed a 'cartography', using statistical analysis to investigate chemical compositions of 14,000 stars through Spectroscopic data from APOGEE. Our study employed a Two-Mechanism Model (TMM) that decomposes observed elemental abundances into contributions from 'cosmic ray nucleosynthesis' and 'mass loss/nuclear burning' components, with residual values indicating deviations from this assumption. Our analysis focused on six elements and stellar ages ranging from 0.5 to 12 billion years, revealing that TMM decomposition patterns vary across different galactic regions and that residual quantities provide insights into individual star's evolutionary history, as well as anomalies in their chemical compositions. Our findings highlight the potential of the TMM as a robust analytical tool in studying stellar and milky way's chemical evolution, while also offering precise location information for the studied stars within the galaxy.

A study was conducted to model the spread of online rumors in real-time during the COVID-19 pandemic in China, focusing on public health-related news. A Susceptible-Locator-Rumour-resister (SLR) framework was developed and applied to analyze data from China. The model accurately predicted the majority of rumor spread patterns, with the exception of two cases with incomplete information. A log-linear regression was used to examine how various factors, including prior knowledge, influenced the propagation of rumors. The study's findings highlight the critical role of prior knowledge in influencing the spread of online information, including news and rumors. Additionally, it was found that urban areas with higher population densities tend to experience more extensive spread of online content, while rural areas are more prone to the spread of rumors. The implications of these findings are further explored in relation to mitigating the negative effects of online information and addressing health-related misinformation.

A human-centric approach to redshifting the Fornax cluster has been initiated through the Fornax3D project, with a focus on precise distance measurements. A key aspect of this project is an open-source spectral analysis tool called SPACTO, which will be utilized to determine the distances to galaxies within the cluster. A comprehensive list of planetary nebulae within these galaxies, previously compiled by various researchers, has been assembled as input data for SPACTO to process. These nebulae's spectral data, historically obtained using film and digital spectroscopy, were discovered through manual inspection and now form the basis for calculating the galaxies' distances. The spectral data associated with these planetary nebulae have been mapped to the NOIRLab EMOS3 simulation facility for SPACTO to utilize. The previously compiled planetary nebulae list and associated spectral data will be publicly released as accompanying data for the SPACTO code. The precise distance measurements results will be publicly accessible and serve as input data for the Fornax3D project. The implementation of SPACTO and its reliance on planetary nebulae distances to determine the galaxies' positions within the cluster were tested using the Local Group, with initial results showing a level of accuracy comparable to existing methods. The public nature of SPACTO and its versatility in utilizing planetary nebulae spectra from different simulation facilities have been highlighted, with a note that its current implementation of Monte Carlo spectral modeling may be replaced with a more efficient alternative, such as SPLAT

Every day, people rely on a vast array of digital applications that generate continuous streams of data, from social media feeds and financial reports to vehicle telemetry and medical monitoring systems. To make sense of these unending flows, machine learning models and sophisticated algorithms are employed, but they place significant computational demands on mobile and other resource-constrained devices. Although previous studies have successfully integrated machine learning and rule-based logic for simple, one-time data analyses, existing frameworks struggle to handle recurring flow operations efficiently. In response, we introduce LifeStream, a novel stream processing framework designed to streamline periodic data flows seamlessly on mobile devices. LifeStream excels at combining machine learning models and R programs for recurring flow operations, excelling at outperforming the renowned Apache Beam framework by notable margins. In fact, lifeStream demonstrates speed improvements of up to 23 times compared to its predecessor, with an average speedup of 10 times.

This research paper confirms a previous finding by K. T. Çerçioğlu and T. Küçükdereli (2013) which states that in Minkowskian 4-space, $R_1^4$, all timelike Bertrand curves are either circular helices or specific types of curve combinations known as helix-helix or catenary-hyperbola curves.

The primary objective of a deep learning classifier is to rank data points according to a predefined order, for example, from most to least similar to the central prototype. This approach is well-suited for handling outlier labels due to its robust ranking capability. In contrast, the standard deep learning training method based on the cross-entropy loss function fails to encourage outlier detection, as it equally values all data points regardless of their status as prototypes or outliers. To address this limitation, we conducted an experimental analysis of how modifying the loss function can enhance the model's ability to identify outliers among data points. Our findings indicate that incorporating a spatial density loss can lead to the automatic identification of outliers during the training process, for instance, by rejecting instances with erroneously labeled data. This result is demonstrated through multiple tasks including image classification and tabular data classification. Furthermore, we believe this approach has potential applications in other areas such as medical or industrial settings where automatic outlier detection is crucial.

This research investigates the strain-induced crystallization processes in polymers using advanced numerical methods. The combination of chemical and mechanical phenomena requires rigorous numerical simulations to fully understand its intricate development. A new numerical framework has been established to simulate these processes, employing a thermodynamically consistent model that accounts for the chemical potential and mechanical stress-stress conjugacy with crystalline fraction, along with finite strain elasticity theory and irreversible crystallization dynamics. The numerical discretization utilizes a specific time-integration scheme and finite element discretization, ensuring accurate and reliable simulation results. Demonstrative simulations have been conducted to illustrate induced crystallization both under sudden stress conditions and during gradual compression, showcasing detailed microstructure developments and liquid-crystal fiber orientations resulting from these processes.

To analyze the impact of Pauli paramagnetism of triplet Cooper pairs on the magnetic susceptibility of nematic superconductors, we formulated a theory based on the self-consistency of the Pauli paramagnetic response and the linearized gap equation for a triplet nematic superconductor near the transition temperature. It was initially developed for a $d_{x^2-y^2}$-wave order parameter and later generalized to an arbitrary symmetry type. We considered two models of nematicity: one where the symmetry breaking arises from the crystal lattice structure and another where it results from electronic interactions. The implications of the local magnetic field modification caused by the triplets on the magnetic susceptibility were also analyzed. Calculations were carried out for a specific nematic and $d_{x^2-y^2}$-superconductor, corresponding to Ba$_{1-x}$K$_{1+x}$CuO$_4$ at $x=0.3$, to validate the model.

A differential continuous-phase modulation (CPM) detection method is improved to allow for a greater difference in time between symbol samples without significantly reducing detection accuracy. This can be seen as a form of encoding that is not strictly tied to a specific scheme, providing the flexibility to choose any detection method, even one that is not aware of changing data patterns. This paper also includes simulation results to support the findings.

The concept of temperature in quantum field theory presents a paradox, as a non-zero temperature implies the existence of photons and the breakdown of a pristine vacuum. This puzzle can be resolved by recognizing that the local definition of temperature is ambiguous in spacetime and its interpretation depends on the observer's perspective. This paper conducts a comprehensive analysis of the quantum stress-energy tensor's fluctuations in various thermal environments, including de Sitter space, asymptotically flat spacetime, and the early universe's radiation-filled phase. Comparing these fluctuations to those in the Rindler wedge helps identify the most and least credible interpretations of "temperature" and defines a new category of spacetime that exhibits both compressibility and quantum capabilities, akin to a quantum gas, even in the absence of a rest frame.

Recent advances in large language models have largely relied on symbolic knowledge, yet creating these models manually is both time-consuming and expensive. Our research introduces ATOMIC, an extensive dataset comprising nearly 1.7 million problem-reasoning pair pairs, where problems are text-based questions and reasoning is an accompanying justification. ATOMIC focuses on simple causal reasoning, categorized into four aspects: observation, goal, plan, and consequence, all centered on common-sense knowledge. Our analysis of text frequency reveals that larger language models benefit most from ATOMIC, particularly when pre-trained on web data. Consequently, we designed a tailored domain-specific subset of ATOMIC, which further demonstrates improved performance. Furthermore, our research establishes that incorporating structural knowledge can enable advanced AI to perform reasoning tasks.

In an increasingly digital and data-driven world, Investment Portfolio Management stands out as a significant challenge and opportunity in the financial industry. Investment firms strive to deliver superior results to their clients while navigating the complexities of traditional and quantitative strategies. Near-term quantum technology has made notable strides in various aspects of finance, including forecasting, pricing derivatives, and evaluating credit risks. To assess the potential of quantum technology in portfolio management comprehensively, we introduce a novel n-step Portfolio Optimization Algorithm. We demonstrate how quantum portfolio optimization can address multi-period Portfolio Management challenges and provide a practical application by reimagining an alpha generation strategy known as Programmatic Advertising. Additionally, we present a Portfolio Enhancement Framework to guide the integration of quantum technology into existing systems. Our findings suggest that a quantum-enabled programmatic advertising strategy outperforms its classical counterpart in terms of ROI, Sharpe ratio, and the level of risk associated with varying time horizons.

In processing multi-modal data, each modality has unique characteristics that should be considered individually.  It's also been observed that many current multi-modal models use unidirectional models like LSTMs, which may not be the most effective approach.  This paper presents a new network called the Bidirectional Focus (BFOCUS) that leverages two separate attention models to select the most relevant parts of each input sequence independently.  We then combine this new attention mechanism with a standard LSTM-based encoder-decoder framework and extend it to handle both speech and text inputs.  To further improve our multi-modal sequence to sequence task, we introduce a vocabulary alignment loss function.  This function helps to align the source and target vocabularies by leveraging the fact that they are derived from the same source data.  We test our approach on the LIBRITTS training and LIBRITTS-2 development datasets and compare our results with those of existing state-of-the-art methods.  We also conduct ablation studies to better understand the individual contributions of each component in our network.

This paper investigates the limiting behavior of uniform initial position configurations for parking functions of length n as n approaches infinity. By analyzing this scenario, we determine the asymptotic distribution, mean, and standard deviation of these initial position configurations. Furthermore, we establish an exact calculation method for probability generating functions that provide comprehensive information about the parking distribution. To support these findings, we also conducted simulation experiments to validate our results. A key component of our analysis involves developing recursive relations for two critical sequences of numbers whose structures offer valuable insights into the analysis. Ultimately, we derive an integral representation for these sequences of numbers.

A study of superconducting nanowires made of NbN nanowires with a 50 nm width and varying lengths conducted at 200 mK reveals a range of behaviors controlled by a gate voltage. As the carrier density changes, the nanowires transition from non-superconducting to Andreev coherent quantum phase slip superconducting conductivity. Conductivity oscillations observed around the transition point indicate a transition threshold that can be as low as 10V/gate. The researchers found that disorder levels in the nanowires cause variation in critical currents and dispersion of cosine-like behavior oscillations can be attributed to quantum interference within the nanowires. The study provides an in-depth analysis of the transition from COOP to CSPS in narrow superconducting nanowires.

Utilizing video data to predict future video views is essential for various applications, including promoting underrepresented activities and avoiding risky ones. Despite this, utilizing video footage to forecast future video views is an underexplored field. To fill this gap, we present a flexible framework that integrates visual content with metadata for video forecasting, allowing for the use of diverse data sources and effectively managing missing values. We apply this framework by combining video clips with associated metadata to forecast future video activities. Our results show that our method outperforms existing techniques, demonstrating its efficacy in accurately forecasting future video events.

The successful application of electron correlation concepts, initially developed for inner-shell electrons, to outer valence electrons has been confirmed through an inter-orbital interaction being observed and measured between $s$ and $p$ electrons in helium's $1s2p$ excited state. Through a thorough analysis of this atom, researchers have determined that ignoring inter-orbital interaction can lead to large mistakes when calculating various properties of one-electron states in He, H, and other similar systems. This conclusion is supported by accurate comparisons made with experimental data and high-quality calculations.

The Ω-baryon, which has been theoretically predicted for over seven decades but only recently observed, holds significant importance in the study of strange quarks due to its constituent quarks and unique properties.  
A key aspect of the Ω-baryon that has been largely neglected comprises its spectroscopic properties, particularly its vibrational, radiative, and rotational modes, which contain abundant information about the dynamics of strange quarks and are highly relevant for developing reliable equations of importance in the study of strange quark matter and quark-gluon plasma in the context of heavy-ion collisions.  
A review of the Ω-baryon's spectral characteristics, including its excitation energies and production mechanisms, is presented, while also highlighting the relevant applications and our current understanding, as well as areas that remain unclear, in order to clarify the dynamics of strange quarks and their role in various phenomena.

A down-to-earth analytical approach is applied to model disease transmission in urban bus networks. Our study contrasts two mathematical frameworks: one incorporating well-mixed dynamics and another more complex one accounting for pairwise interactions. Our analysis reveals the simpler model accurately captures key epidemiological features of the spread of infectious diseases in these networks. The simpler model correctly estimates critical thresholds and effective sizes of the network, providing a useful tool for estimating intervention effects of measures like increasing cleaning frequencies or reducing fleet sizes. The simpler model also facilitates a clearer interpretation of empirical regression outcomes obtained when evaluating such effects.

This study investigates the spin-orbit effects in Cobalt/Bismuth multilayer films using both theoretical and experimental approaches. Noticing that Cobalt exhibits a notably low spin-orbit splitting, we explored how introducing Bismuth layers might enhance this characteristic, potentially enabling the realization of the inverse spin Hall effect in such materials. Unexpectedly, we found that Bismuth/Cobalt multilayers fail to display the anticipated inverse spin Hall effect, likely due to the converse spin Hall effect's presence in this configuration, as confirmed by the Ru/Cb and Pt/Cb comparisons. A critical finding is that the magnitude of the inverse spin Hall effect is heavily influenced by the scattering at the interface between the layers, allowing for a precise calculation of the spin-orbit coupling through engineering the Bismuth/Cobalt film thickness, as verified by our experimental results.

This research presents exact solutions to the time-independent fractional Schrödinger equation in various generalized Mie-like potentials across multiple dimensions. The study assumes a non-relativistic, fractional dynamics framework and involves potential functions such as generalized Mie, Mie, and Coulomb-Mie. The methods employed utilize Jumarie type fractional derivatives, which lack a commutative property with the derivative operator in radial parts of the wave function. The obtained solutions enable the determination of corresponding energy eigenvalues and corresponding wave functions. Additionally, the study provides a numerical analysis of the expected values for the radius in various dimensions and fractional orders. The findings are relevant to the fields of quantum physics, optical physics, and quantum mechanics.

Overfitting in deep neural networks often manifests as high variance in predictions, especially in regions of the input space far from training data. Our research indicates that reducing the network's function to a sufficiently smooth variety can significantly improve general performance. We propose a method for estimating a network's "generalization capacity" using the Kolmogorov–Laptev Lipschitz constant, leading to a corresponding regularization technique that effectively controls this capacity. Our capacity penalty is computationally efficient to calculate and optimize, allowing for large mini-batches and efficient GPU utilization. Furthermore, this method can be applied to both classification and regression network types. Our capacity regularization technique outperforms competing methods in various benchmarks, demonstrating better results with neural networks that exhibit a smaller generalization capacity for datasets such as MNIST, SVHN, and CIFAR-10.

We investigate the Drell-Yan production of colorless lepton-quark pairs at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). This phenomenon, theoretically possible, arises from specific leptoquark models, specifically those involving top quark decay and violating certain conservation laws. By examining different leptoquark models - namely the charged, neutral, and colourless third-generation gauge vector leptoquarks - and calculating their cross-sections at NLO in QCD, we found the primary sources of uncertainty in our predictions to be the choice of factorization and renormalization scales, with an estimated variation of approximately 20%. Although this process is suppressed by a factor of $10^{-5}$ compared to the standard top-quark decay channel, it may become observable with high-luminosity LHC runs, potentially allowing for the discovery of these leptoquarks before their signature appears in the actual top-quark decay data.

Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans is minimized by lowering the number of detected photons, but this increases the level of noise in the resulting images and limits their detail. Advanced deep learning models have been developed to reduce noise in low-quality PET images by utilizing associated CT images as references, achieving improved results compared to single-modality methods. However, these models often struggle when the relationship between PET and CT images does not conform to expected patterns, particularly when encountering data outside their training distribution. This paper introduces a novel neural network framework that utilizes Bayesian neural networks to explicitly model uncertainty in PET-CT image reconstruction, allowing for more accurate and robust results, even when the expected relationship between the images is not present. Experimental evaluations show that this method produces high-quality reconstructions with accurate uncertainty estimates, resulting in reduced detection of false positives and better performance in various downstream tasks such as semantic segmentation and CT prediction from reduced-dose PET scans. This approach provides a consistent and reliable solution for joint PET-CT reconstruction by leveraging the strengths of both single-modality and multi-modality methods while minimizing their respective limitations.

According to Rogers and Friedman's centring theory (1988, 1990), an utterance's meaning is determined not just by its grammatical components, but also by the contextual information from the conversation or text. Central entities in the discourse are more likely to be referred to pronouns than peripheral entities. This research investigates if centring theory's proposed structural relationships can aid in solving coreference problems using a mix of textual information and context dependencies. Our primary finding reveals that certain context dependencies align with centring theory's predictions, helping to resolve coreference. However, we also discovered that more distant context dependencies contradict the theory's predictions. To address this, we developed a modified centring model that yields improved results in multiway coreference within the Wikipedia context.

The underlying network of WiFi has been utilized for various indoor positioning tasks, such as navigating for vehicles and delivering packages, due to its ability to provide distance estimates between devices. Although initial methods for estimating distances between WiFi devices relied on signal strength information, such as Time of Arrival or Amplitude, they were highly susceptible to errors caused by obstacles like walls and furniture, which are prevalent in real-world environments. As a result, accurate distance estimates became nearly unattainable without the use of intrusive and costly equipment, such as ultrasonic sensors or GPS. However, our current proposal leverages the existing WiFi infrastructure to generate accurate estimates of the distance between devices utilizing it, utilizing a deep learning technique known as Neural Networks. Although this method produces accurate results, it also incorporates the inclusion of non-line-of-sight phenomena, allowing the system to effectively navigate real-world obstacles without the use of intrusive sensors.

We investigate the beam disruption phenomenon, also known as BRDI, that occurs in energy recovery linacs based on the configuration of the storage ring. This type of instability arises from an intense, high-gradient electromagnetic pulse interacting with pipe wall impedance, potentially leading to beam loss and possible damage to superconducting cavities. Research indicates that an self-consistent analysis accounting for energy loss, radiation, and configuration of the SRLINAC system is necessary to address this instability. This paper presents simulations of an test scenario at CESR-INJINAC system showing that, under certain conditions, even a low level of RID can result in significant particle loss and damage to the radio frequency cavity. Furthermore, paper provides an analysis of several strategies for mitigating this effect.

To extend the $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills four-glueball amplitude to one-loop level, we developed a virtual-parton impact factor, denoted as $\mathcal{F}_A$, in the double-regime where two glueballs with very small transverse sizes remain collinearly invariant. Specifically, $\mathcal{F}_A$ was derived within the high-energy limit where the longitudinal momenta of the two glueballs, $p_{1,2}$, are considered to be in the massless limit, $p_{1,2}^2 \approx 0$, and their transverse sizes, $\rho_{1,2}$, are very small, $\rho_{1,2} \ll 1$. This derivation was performed within the KMBC-KMR formalism. We discovered that $\mathcal{F}_A$ comprises a one-loop correction to the KMBC-KMR impact factor from hadronization of a single colorless scalar boson, denoted as $\sigma_F$, multiplied by a dimensionless coefficient, denoted as $\mathcal{K}_A$, i.e., $\mathcal{F}_A = \sigma_F \mathcal{K}_A$. This research focuses on developing a mathematical model to analyze the friction characteristics of an arbitrary surface, taking into account the behavior of polymer bristles in a molten state and subject to significant tension. Our approach involves re-establishing the integrity of a previously proposed model, incorporating the dynamics of polymer molecules into our framework, and utilizing it to determine specific parameters. Furthermore, we extend our scheme to map the structural characteristics of surfaces in relation to their frictional properties for surfaces characterized by molten, heavily stretched polymer bristles. Our analysis highlights three distinct zones for these surfaces: a zone where the shape of the surface is inconsequential, a zone where the degree of tension influences the structure of the surface, and a zone where the surface is stretched beyond its original form. In addition, we investigate the transition between the first two zones and discover that a specific relationship influences the tension required to enter the "arbitrary shape" zone, independent of the surface's initial state. Our research yields several mathematical relations that can be applied to improve the understanding and prediction of the frictional characteristics of surfaces with molten, heavily stretched polymer brilles and the state of a fourth "oligomer brush" end exclusion zone that has been hitherto unrecognized.

A subset of vertices in a graph G is considered resolvable when, for every vertex w in the graph, the distance vectors from a specific subset V to w are distinct. The smallest size of such a resolvable subset is referred to as the metric dimension of the graph. This concept is then extended to directed graphs and weighted graphs. In the case of directed graphs, a subset V is considered resolvable when, for every vertex w in the graph, the directed distance vectors from V to w are distinct. For weighted graphs, a subset V is considered resolvable when, for every vertex w in the graph, the actual shortest path lengths from V to w are distinct. The smallest size of such a resolvable subset is referred to as the shortened metric dimension of the graph. The concepts of directionally determined and strongly determined graphs are also defined in relation to the shortened metric dimension. Some initial investigations into the properties of the shortened metric dimension for various types of graphs, including complete graphs, star graphs, paths, and trees, are explored.

A luminous all-sky map is created using Fermi-LAT data from 11 years, incorporating 15 MeV to 300 GeV energy range. As a result, a precise catalog of galaxies, clusters, and cosmic rays is generated. Because of the broad energy range, source resolution is improved at both lower and higher energy thresholds. A high energy all-sky chart at 3 GeV to 300 GeV is also produced for comparison. Interestingly, a correlation is observed between the two chart types as most structures appear consistently in both. Nevertheless, some sources are newly identified in the high energy chart that have not been detected in the standard all-sky map. A potential reason for this discrepancy, likely related to new physics, is speculated based on the absence of these sources in the standard all-sky chart.

A serial dictatorship mechanism is one in which agents take turns submitting
their most preferred feasible allocations up to a certain point, with the
last agent submitting their most preferred feasible allocation, effectively
mimicking a dictatorship mechanism from a specific agent.  We introduce a
enhanced model of serial dictatorships where some agents are permitted to
submit non-monotone functions within their respective domains.  We establish
this model's equivalence to generalized agent-based implementations and
revealed-preferences implementations.  However, unlike this model, general
agent-based implementations and revealed-preferences implementations require
agents to undergo repeated interactions.  Moreover, Generalized Serial
Dictatorships provide a clearer understanding of which functions can be
effectively implemented through single-shot implementations and which cannot.

We developed a novel technique to detect binary asteroids individually imaged across multiple epochs, utilizing historical Pan-STARRS1 data. This method relies on analyzing the movement of the primary asteroid and its companion in the plane of sky, using astrometric information extracted from two images taken at different times. After compiling and refining our dataset, it was found that approximately 1 in 4,000 variable light curves corresponds to a binary system, resulting in the discovery of 13 new asteroids with confirmed binary systems: 2015 EH25, 2014 CW108, 2013 UU114, 2014 AZ140, 2014 AR138, 2012 UU154, 2014 EZ133, 2013 UU145, 2014 EZ130, 2012 UU140, and two revisions of previously identified systems, 2009 AZ142 and 2011 AZ150, with respective semi-major axes of 0.333 arcseconds for 2015 EH25, 0.363 arcseconds for 2014 CW108, 0.393 arcseconds for 2013 UU114, 0.243 arc

This work introduces a general statistical model that combines linear and non-linear components and incorporates network information for a set of variables. We develop an estimator to assess the non-linear part of the model, examining its impact using simulated network data and establishing consistency under heteroskedastic conditions. Furthermore, we create a robust covariance matrix estimator, valid under general conditions regarding the variables. A secondary application explores network peer effects in the context of state variables represented by binary indicators, resulting in a new econometric model and corresponding estimation technique.

This study develops a framework for a generalized Leibniz Theorem tailored to the Riemann-Liouville variable-order fractional integral and derivative operator, extending upon earlier findings. Our theorem expresses the product's behavior under the product rule for the fractional operator when applied to the product of two differentiable functions, highlighting unique properties in contrast to its constant-order counterpart. In particular, our result demonstrates that applying the fractional operator to the product of functions yields an outcome that is neither purely additive nor multiplicative. To illustrate, our theoretical results provide a direct extension of previous findings, including those where the variable order is a concave function, leading to orders less than one and thus making the product differentiable only in the leading edge of the integration range.

This paper presents the AI Dungeon Master (IDM) framework, which aims to lead players through a theory-of-mind-based social interaction that mimics a Dungeons and Dragons game. As an advanced iteration of an AI Dungeon Master, the IDM has two main components: an intent engine that uses a revised version of the common sense reasoning (CSR) framework to anticipate and plan for theoretical outcomes, and a game engine that prepares and executes physical actions within the game world. To demonstrate the effectiveness of the IDM, we conducted a simulation of a D&D game using both prepared and improvised responses, with positive feedback from experienced players. The results indicate high satisfaction with the IDM's knowledge, its ability to lead the game, its use of humor, and its ability to engage in meaningful social interaction with the players.

The intricate folding and knotting patterns in proteins are essential for executing their functions, yet the underlying mechanisms driving this process remain elusive. Kinetic studies reveal that proteins evolve under constraints, with knots being associated with functional significance and precursors to knotting being linked to functional states. Prior research has relied on simulated mutations to identify knots and potential precursors through contact patterns, but these approaches are arbitrary and do not reflect the natural occurrence of mutations. In contrast, the topological consequences of mutations can be objectively assessed using mathematical tools, revealing that the amino acid arrangements influencing knotting patterns are more fundamental than previously thought. Through a case study of the yeast escherichia coli nucleoid-associated protein (NupA), research demonstrates that the non-specific knotting patterns in NupA result from the natural arrangement of its domains, with a more open configuration facilitating the entanglement of its globular domains.

We establish that for any positive integer $n \geq 1$, the symplectic mapping class group of the blowup of a $4n$-dimensional toroid in a four-dimensional symplectic manifold is not residually finite.

A Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem exists in both relativistic and nonrelativistic quantum field theory (QFT) contexts. This paper explores the general form of the NG theorem, showing how it accounts for various phenomena such as spontaneous symmetry breaking, the appearance of massless pions in quantum chromodynamics (QCD), and the occurrence of massive pions. We illustrate our points with several examples, including the linear sigma model, the Anderson-Higgs mechanism, and the effective field theory of pions. Notably, we show how the NG theorem implies the masslessness of pions in the limit where quark masses are negligible. We also discuss the implications of the NG theorem for the effective field theory of quarks.

Deep learning models can sometimes produce accurate results by mimicking patterns without truly understanding the underlying content, compared to humans who expect to be able to grasp and learn from counterfactual statements, which provide new information and knowledge. This study investigates whether the internal mechanisms of large language models, specifically the mid-layer activations of their artificial neural networks, capture a representation that allows them to generalize effectively and provide explanations for their predictions and engage in reasoning. Experimental findings reveal that these mid-layer representations and a simple classification model can distinguish between words and phrasal counterfactuals across various transformation types and document directories, accurately predicting the original labels of counterfactual texts and offering counterfactual explanations for both predictions and results from random mid-layer projections. Moreover, we demonstrate that these representations capture a concept of causality, which can be utilized to make more robust predictions that are less susceptible to adversarial attacks and able to solve complex tasks, such as solving math problems presented to elementary school students. Finally, we release the dataset utilized in this study to ensure reproducibility of results.

Enlisting remote epitaxy in graphene-covered sapphire substrates to create novel electronic applications requires overcoming tightly confined van der Waals epitaxy. Through experiments and theoretical understanding, we've developed pinhole and remote epitaxy models to complement the well-known van der Waals and native epitaxy models. Researching the four epitaxy models on a specific heusler film CdP2, we identified direct correlations between dominant epitaxy models and various phenomena occurring on the film's surface. Notably, remote epitaxy gave rise to step-nucleation at terrace boundaries, step-bending, and spiral nucleation, whereas van der Waals epitaxy resulted in layer-by-layer growth and domain formation. Furthermore, we discovered that remote epitaxy growth contributes uniquely to the asymmetric magnetization of canting within the heusler film's spindles. To facilitate epitaxy engineering, we created a unified model incorporating surface and van der Waals forces, demonstrating that remote, pinhole, and van der Waals epitaxy forces can be independently manipulated to facilitate novel heusler growth patterns on sapphire substrates covered in graphene.

Let $f$ be a prime number greater than 3. This research examines the characteristics of $\mathbb{Z}_f\mathbb{Z}_{f^2}}$-linear codes, focusing on their imposed free structure and exploring their underlying geometry in relation to codes with imposed symmetries. The study reveals that codes with such symmetries can be understood as subcodes of $\mathbb{Z}_f$-linear codes, which may have an optimal minimum distance according to established coding theory standards. Furthermore, it provides methods for increasing the minimum distance of $\mathbb{Z}_f$-linear codes by identifying and removing subcodes with imposed symmetries that have an minimum distance of at least a certain value. The research also presents erasure resistant $\mathbb{Z}_5\mathbb{Z}_{25}}$-linear codes, which can achieve a semi-optimal minimum distance and have an unusually high dimension relative to their constituent parts and minimum distance according to existing coding theory standards.

In the context of improving supervised models for imbalanced datasets, leveraging unlabeled data through co-training has shown notable success. Such approaches implicitly assume that labels represent single-classifications, meaning one label per instance corresponds to a single class. This work explores the possibility of enriching the unlabeled dataset by identifying multi-label instances within the data. Such instances, where one label encompasses multiple classes, can be leveraged to explicitly train the classifiers, thereby expanding the range of useful unlabeled data and facilitating implicit multi-label expansion. Our proposed framework, ReLabel, utilizes a simple yet robust method to detect multi-label instances and assigns them accordingly. When applied to the CIFAR-10 dataset with varying levels of class imbalance, our method showed substantial gains in performance compared to a baseline that uses only labeled data. Furthermore, our findings reveal that multi-label instances are frequently prevalent in data that contains single-label classifications.

We construct a robust and adaptable framework for Hilbert space formation using 2-presheaves, which we then use to demonstrate the adjacency of formation of linear structures and subsequent presheaves over arbitrary base categories. This adjacency is particularly beneficial in establishing algebraic theories through functors that preserve specific coherence structures. We effectively apply this adjacency to establish the formation of semi-normed vector spaces from their constituent parts - a normed vector space formation adjunction.

We investigate the high-energy gamma-ray signals from magnetohydrodynamic disks captured in intense magnetic fields within radio galaxies. When these galaxies reside in the nearby universe where extragalactic gamma rays can reach us, we expect to observe them as energy peaks. We simulate the gamma-ray distributions for both steady and time-varying disk conditions under the influence of extreme magnetic fields, and compare them to the energy spectra of photons passing through magnetic fields. A series of gamma-ray images are generated for radio galaxies under different magnetic field orientations and configurations. The predicted gamma-ray signals from these models match the characteristics recently observed from spiral galaxies, such as NGC 4258, previously undetected in gamma rays. It's also proposed that gamma rays from captured disks could enhance the energy efficiency of some spiral galaxies, like NGC 4258, and that monitoring these galaxies with gamma rays could provide insights into their core magnetic fields and disk dynamics.

A noisy environment during medical tests like echocardiograms leads to image distortion and extra lines, making medical image analysis more difficult for professionals. In addition, it can result in inaccurate diagnoses. This study presents a method to classify heart conditions using noisy and distorted echocardiograms, which involves classifying heart sounds that are often used in cardiac disease detection. This method achieves an 87% accuracy in heart sound classification, exceeding the current achievable accuracy of 75% to 80% with similar techniques, even with low-resolution, noisy data.

The rapid expansion of healthcare data and the spread of wearable technology create significant potential for machine learning models to make a meaningful impact in the medical field. However, sensitive patient data protection issues and the scarcity of accurately labeled images hinder the development and deployment of such models. This paper presents FedHealth, a novel framework that combines federated learning and transfer learning to address these challenges and pave the way for future wearable medical diagnostics. FedHealth can train robust models on hospitals' localized health data and can be utilized to enhance predictions on wearable device data. Evaluations on real-world datasets reveal that FedHealth outperforms traditional learning approaches and has the capability to produce reliable models for wearable monitoring. Furthermore, the framework's versatility allows it to be adapted across diverse medical applications.

Various series, including random walks, have been found to exhibit when analyzed with a specific approach involving sorted values. This study establishes a connection between the behavior of these series, particularly in relation to random walks, and the results of certain portfolio optimization methods, including those based on covariance matrix estimation, can also be linked to the results of these analyses. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a range of portfolio techniques when analyzed produce results similar to the sorted values of returns, also known as heavy-tailed distributions, it is suggested that the results of these analyses provide a theoretical foundation for the inefficiencies observed in financial markets, including the effectiveness of momentum strategies and the limited performance of models in risk management applications, also highlighting the influence of these techniques on a variety of applications beyond portfolio optimization, including derivatives pricing and capital market assessments, ultimately providing a unified approach to understanding various issues in capital markets through the concepts of scaled values, sorted returns, and elevated moments.
