This study investigates the impact of a unique operation called the toggling control in a specific type of financial problem, related to stopping times and involving cost functions that exhibit right-continuous and non-increasing characteristics on a time scale. Our main achievement is demonstrating that an alternative formulation of the toggling control issue, initially put forward by Bayraktar and Song (2022), can be equivalently used in the given context, even with non-monotone cost functions, thereby resolving an outstanding challenge stated in their work. Furthermore, we establish additional results including optimal strategies that may involve exiting and re-entering a state.

To explain the mechanism of neutrino generation observed in experiments, a specific type of leptoquark theory is considered, which features two scalar leptoquarks operating at varying energy scales. Researchers have developed effective field theories for both scenarios where the higher-energy leptoquark dominates, carefully analyzing flavor-changing processes involving charged leptons and applying them to searches conducted by the LHC. These studies focus on signatures involving same-sign lepton pairs along with jets and missing energy. A comparable effective field theory is also established for scenarios with a single leptoquark type. By incorporating both theories, an analysis of experimental data from the CMS on LHC runs at 8 TeV and 13 TeV is performed. This analysis yields constraints on the energy scales and coupling constants based on observed events. A specific example is examined in which two leptoquarks interact with a new force, governed by a SU(2) gauge group, drawing comparisons to previous leptoquark research. This example sets energy scale limits for a new physics occurrence with a cross-section comparable to experimental observations, often in the range of a few picobarns.

Computing the detailed structure of galaxies relies on knowledge of their gas composition and movement. Spectra from submillimeter lines provide key insights into gas temperature and movement, though many lines may not accurately reflect the gas temperature due to their low excitation, especially for complex molecules. Although this issue is manageable for simple atoms and molecules, it complicates interpretations and remains poorly quantified. This research uses Monte Carlo simulations to assess the extent of subthermal saturation for the cyanogen (CI) lines, a tool that offers a consistent reference for further gas reservoir analysis. Simulations account for various conditions found within galaxies, offering guidance on using CI lines to characterize gas composition and temperature. A new, dimensionless parameter is proposed to predict the degree of CI line saturation across different environments, aligning closely with simulation outcomes. This parameter integrates key factors such as gas reservoir microturbulence and external radiation effects. Despite their low energy, CI lines offer valuable information about gas composition and can be used to compare different galaxies or regions within a single galaxy.

A key metric for distinguishing hypergraphs is the Hamming distance between them. This distance measures the number of edges in the symmetric difference between two hypergraphs when one is transformed into the other via coordinate flips in a binary space. A key property of hypergraphs is reconstructability from a sequence of adjacent hypergraphs that cover all possible hypergraphs in the space. It has been established that graphs and circles are reconstructible from such sequences, but a pattern isn't clear for other hypergraphs. A challenge was set in 2020 to determine if arrangements with the Hamming distance are reconstructible from such sequences, but it was shown in 2021 that smaller arrangements with the same number of arrangements are not reconstructible in general. This paper continues the investigation into the reconstruction problem for arrangements with the Hamming distance.

Researchers anticipate using pulsar timing arrays to detect low-frequency gravitational waves in the near future. These signals could provide insights into the supermassive binary black hole population. To accurately model potential timing array data and a variety of waveform models are now required, which must account for relativistic effects and vary based on binary systems' orbital eccentricity. Recently introduced models, including those based on Taylor expansions and two-body dynamics, parameter space extensions, and multiple-signal simulations, have various limitations. This study comprehensively analyzes these models' efficiency and accuracy, particularly in relation to observing eccentricity. The results reveal that while some models offer high precision with low computational costs for small to moderate eccentricities, others may introduce unnecessary errors or significantly increase computational expenses. This analysis of model performance will be crucial in preparing for future analyses of potential pulsar timing array discoveries.

We establish that the velocity process of an Asymmetric Simple Exclusion Random Walk, ASEP, on the integer line constitutes a Markov process. Taking any initial configuration, we demonstrate that the velocity process up to a random time, determined by an exponential distribution with rate one, follows the same distribution as the full velocity process. This method enables us to precisely define a comprehensive family of non-local stochastic processes, each corresponding to a different interaction rate at will.

Comprehensive epidemic models have been published within one and a half months of the first reported cases in Italy, with these models spanning various complexities. These models range from basic versions suitable for brief presentations to highly detailed formulations ideal for in-depth research. This brevity in which these models were released underscores their straightforward nature. This brief timeframe highlights their adaptable nature. 

Furthermore, during this same period, these models were effectively utilized to support the emerging public discourse on the epidemic, with versions of these models being utilized in the media and on social media platforms. This utility of these models was evident in their application in public discussions. 

However, upon reviewing the literature surrounding these models, notable discrepancies arise between their mathematical simplicity and their apparent suitability for statistical inference. This contrast between their perceived applicability and their limiting assumptions is particularly striking given their suggested use in statistical analysis. This evident difference between these models' stated intentions and their underlying limitations is particularly noteworthy. 

Although this review focuses on the current epidemic, its principles are broadly applicable to other outbreaks as well. This applicability of this review beyond the current context is particularly valuable for its lasting relevance.

We have theoretically analyzed the dynamics of a three-particle system made of an atom-atom pair and a single spin-state different particle, under the conditions of resonant three-body collisions. We show that when a high intensity laser is present, and drives the molecule formed by the two particles at a lossy molecular state, the molecule-loss and single-loss three-body recombination rates become comparable. We provide a formalism and explicit expressions to describe these processes, which occur due to spin-loss on an external trap. We provide an in-depth examination of three-body recombination in spinor gases, uncovering previously unexplored phenomena and potentially usable applications, particularly the under-shelling of molecules and enhancement of molecule-loss rates. We highlight an expanded region where loss mechanisms are dominant, defined by a higher power-law exponent, which could be observable in a wide range of experiments.

This study focuses on constructing efficient hierarchical DNA storage systems to handle frequently updating data within specific partitions. In dynamic datasets, certain sections are subject to frequent revisions, requiring associated hierarchies to be considered. Traditional hierarchical codes, though effective, present performance issues due to their extended DNA sequences. To address this challenge, a new class of asymmetric hierarchical codes is proposed, offering improved code capacity and correction capabilities. The proposed codes' properties are formally proven, while an empirical assessment using an actual DNA storage system demonstrates their practical efficacy in managing frequently updating data. Furthermore, the research explores resolving cross-talk interference in nested data intervals to enhance code performance. The proposed codes' superior attributes are highlighted in comparison to conventional coding solutions, with their theoretical and practical advantages clearly outlined.

We introduce a new hybrid approach that combines traditional finite difference methods with deep learning to create a highly efficient solver for the shallow water equations. This solver, termed D^2LSE, is trained using water depth, flow rate, and elevation data as inputs, and uses them to accurately predict water level, flow velocity, and elevation at given locations. We demonstrate that D^2LSE can rapidly and accurately simulate complex hydrological scenarios, including rapid inundation and erosion, and outperforms conventional finite difference methods in terms of speed. Our approach is shown to be capable of handling large-scale simulations at a fraction of the time required by traditional numerical methods.

HDR images can significantly enhance the dynamic range compared to conventional single exposures, making them ideal for diverse and demanding lighting conditions. This research proposes a robust framework for determining the optimal number of exposures to capture and develops innovative methods for combining images to produce high-quality HDR results. This framework is applicable to a wide range of applications, including the creation of photographs on mobile devices. A key aspect of this research involves collecting a large-scale dataset consisting of professional-grade images paired with their corresponding scenes' dynamic ranges. This extensive dataset enables and motivates several unique, data-driven approaches to exposure selection and HDR fusion. Notably, this research demonstrates that a carefully constructed set of varying exposures can produce superior results to those who freely choose the number of exposures, while also introducing original and effective HDR fusion strategies. To validate the effectiveness of these methods, extensive quantitative and qualitative assessments are conducted, showcasing the proposed framework's versatility, reliability, and overall success.

Deep neural networks have extensively utilized in representing complex data patterns in recent years. However, such success primarily relies on empirical experience without theoretical foundation, especially regarding their capacity to represent causal relationships. Our paper establishes the causal representation hypothesis for deep neural networks, demonstrating that they can accurately reflect causal connections between input and output variables. We first analyze the structural properties of neural networks, revealing how specific components function as nonlinear binary classifiers that construct a fragmented map of the input space. Subsequent simulation experiments further validate our findings and explore their implications.

For a subset W of the projective plane over the set of rational numbers, showing the existence of an infinite collection of plane curves, denoted by F, that intersect every curve in W, was initially established by Jouanolou and Manin for complex numbers and by Harbater, Matzke, and Momose for the set of rational numbers. We provide a collection of examples where the intersection of all curves in F results in a set with a higher dimension than expected, including one example related to the so-called "Mumford problem".

In this study, the efficiency of multiple multilevel preconditioning methods in relation to cardiac mechanics simulations is evaluated. Using a cohesive-spline enhanced mixed assumed mode shape reduction technique, the non-linear finite element equations for viscoelastic cardiac mechanics are solved. This involves a Monte Carlo assessment of the Multilevel Preconditioner variants, including HYPRE, algebraic multigrid (AlbMini and ILBMini), and a multilevel cyclical method, across multiple time integration steps of the constitutive model and equilibrium equations of mechanics. Furthermore, the paper examines the impact of element size, constitutive model parameters, material heterogeneity, and geometry on MP efficiency. Furthermore, the paper establishes empirical scaling laws based on problem dimensions and number of degrees of freedom.

This study investigates the relationship between the spatial distribution of permeability in a 2D Hele-Shaw apparatus and the resulting fluid particle diffusion dynamics. We utilize the synthetic aperture sonar technique to map spatial permeability variations via thickness fluctuations of a transparent acrylic plate with randomly varying depths. Our analysis reveals that fluid diffusion within this device exhibits spatial non-Gaussian characteristics, closely correlated with the statistically fractional Brownian motion pattern of permeability in space. Correlation functions and conditional probability distributions provide strong evidence of this relationship. Furthermore, we establish that spatial non-Gaussian diffusion can induce temporal non-Gaussian diffusion with heavy-tailed probability density functions and long-range temporal correlations, inducing diffusion-tail and diffusion-memory effects respectively.

We developed optical tools, specifically a ring resonator and a waveguide, to experimentally verify and demonstrate spatial image processing capabilities. By analyzing the scattering of light as it moves through these tools, we obtained transmission coefficients that depended on the intensity of light. This allowed us to process optical data in both linear and nonlinear processes at a surprisingly low intensity. As the ring resonator and waveguide interacted with light, they responded according to optical constants that varied with the environment.

A primary goal in fluid dynamics research is measuring turbulent flow patterns, and advancements in measurement technology, especially advanced velocimetry, have produced highly detailed, three-dimensional, and time-varying flow data. Despite these capabilities, such high-resolution data sets remain scarce due to their cost to acquire and are hard to obtain for experiments at higher Reynolds numbers. Researchers have tried collecting high-resolution data sets at various Reynolds numbers, but lower-resolution versions are often easier to acquire or simulate. This study introduces a new, high-resolution, and diverse dataset of turbulent plane mixing layer flow, recorded using advanced velocimetry techniques, and also develops a recovery method based on generative adversarial networks to high-fidelity, and diverse Reynolds number flow fields. The results show that the proposed model accurately predicts high-resolution, and diverse Reynolds number flow fields including the new dataset, and provides a systematic and accurate transformation between lower- and high-resolution flow fields.

Recently, reinforcement learning algorithms have seen significant advancements, 
but their capacity to generalize across diverse tasks remains unclear. Current 
benchmarks primarily assess inter-task generalization, which we differentiate 
from the broader concept of lifelong generalization that encompasses dynamic 
states, actions, and rewards. We present Lifelong Explorer, a novel RL evaluation 
environment featuring ten carefully crafted, non-stagnant tasks spanning various 
domains, including gaming, driving, and robotics. Our environment excludes any 
data filtering or synthetic reward modification, ensuring a rigorous benchmark 
for lifelong generalization research. We provide initial results using several 
state-of-the-art algorithms and gather qualitative insights, suggesting that 
reinforcement learning models can exhibit generalization across diverse, evolving 
tasks. We release Lifelong Explorer as an open-source repository to encourage 
future evaluations and developments.

Process mining combines actual process data with analytical techniques to extract insights and enhance our understanding of processes. In contrast, generative approaches, such as our proposed tree-guided method, leverage mathematical models to create processes. This research combines both approaches by using a process stream to provide information from real processes to a generative model. We've developed a new approach that monitors and improves tree-based generative models of processes. In this method, an evolutionary tree model is used to reproduce a known process, with information extracted from the actual process to refine the model and make exploration processes more purposeful. A key aspect of this framework is the use of probabilistic processes as stream data, with our proposed algorithm demonstrating its effectiveness through various process models and exploration tasks.

This paper gives an overview of compactification methodologies for moduli spaces, focusing on their fundamental properties and key examples. We begin by examining the challenge of creating compactifications and their significance, particularly in applications to physics and the study of dynamical systems. Subsequently, we review various compactification techniques for moduli spaces, highlighting their properties and interconnections. These methods include Hodge-theoretic, Satake compactifications, Borel-Sera and Mumford's geometric compactification. We also provide a more detailed examination of the Mumford compactification.

We used recent large-scale observations with VLT/MUSE of local star-forming galaxies to analyze their component parts in relation to the total galaxies, focusing on spectral energy distributions. These observations allowed us to determine physical properties such as mass formation rates and masses of individual galaxies. We then examined the relationship between masses formation rates and total masses, paying particular attention to how it changes at different mass scales. To further understand this relationship, we compared our findings with simulations and studied individual galaxies. The study revealed that the characteristic point where the relationship starts to differ, previously thought to be caused by suppression of star formation in galaxy centers, is actually influenced by the transition from disk galaxies to those with bulges. The turnover point varies depending on whether a galaxy has a smooth light distribution or contains a bulge, with galaxies having larger bulges showing the relationship plateau at higher specific star formation rates and declining more rapidly than expected. The analysis also highlighted the critical role that mergers play in transforming galaxies and influencing their star formation capabilities.

This research focuses on developing a unified model for cross-lingual sentiment assessment across multiple tasks using both supervised and semi-supervised methods. The primary goal is to classify sentiments in under-resourced languages despite utilizing annotated data from well-documented languages. By leveraging pairwise sentiment labels from source languages, the model aims to enhance representation learning and transfer effective embeddings to target languages with minimal annotation. A key innovation is incorporating a sentiment category prediction task to guide semi-supervised training, resulting in a novel framework called Multi-task Conditional Transfer Learning (MTCTL). Evaluations at the sentence and document levels show that our approach, specifically the MTCTL framework, achieves superior performance in sentiment assessment across various languages including English, German, and Turkish.

Studies on X-ray imaging have been conducted to identify COVID-19, which may be critical for quick and accurate diagnoses in clinical settings. However, these studies often exclude data from patients with severe symptoms requiring intensive care unit admission, which could significantly impact lung imaging. Utilizing publicly available X-ray images of COVID-19 patients, which do not distinguish between mild to moderate and severe cases, we created a dataset and explored potential indicators of ICU admission including age, gender, and other relevant factors. Our analysis revealed that older age was associated with a higher likelihood of severe disease, along with a notable increase in ground opacity in affected lungs. Although further research with larger datasets is necessary, these findings may be valuable for developing more accurate X-ray based severity models for COVID-19 patients.

We establish that the simplicial looping operation preserves the property of being a simplicial group, which leads to the conclusion that a higher stromol group $L^k W$ is indeed a simplicial group for all $k$ and $w$. Furthermore, if a 2-simplicial set $w$ is already a simplicial group, then its higher suspended variants $\Sigma^k W$ maintain this structure for any $k$.

This work focuses on overcoming a significant issue in Visual Relationship Detection(VRD) known as erroneous relationships. Statistics show that approximately 60% of predicted relationships in state-of-the-art models are false. To address this problem, we propose a new framework called Visual Relationship Marginalization(VRM). In this approach, we develop a difficulty score that quantifies the likelihood of a relationship being false given the current visualization of entities. We integrate this score into the training process to effectively train a VRD model. Furthermore, we introduce a novel dataset called Fake-VCO, which contains a large number of falsely predicted relationships along with a few true relationships within a single image. This dataset is specifically designed to challenge current VRD models and enable them to better distinguish between true and false relationships within single images containing two waypoints. When our proposed method is evaluated using the Fake-VCO dataset and compared to the current leading models on widely accepted VRD datasets, it demonstrates a significant reduction in predicted erroneous relationships while maintaining a high level of performance.

We've analyzed the stellar populations of the galaxy AB12496C at the core of a galaxy cluster from over a billion years ago. This involves examining their number, distribution, and individual star formation history of the galaxy's disk, bulge, and central nuclear region. Our findings reveal that the galaxy's disk is lacking in color, slightly reddening towards the center, and exhibits unusual behavior - its inner parts formed stars more vigorously and recently compared to its outer parts. In contrast, the bulge and nuclear region formed fewer stars but formed them continuously over a longer period. By modeling how stars move and interact within the galaxy, we've linked its structural development to various processes like star formation, accretion, and stellar dynamics. This reveals that a large amount of dry gas accretion along a central path could explain the galaxy's unusual star formation pattern. In addition, we've proposed that accretion, quenching, and bar-driven star formation interacted with one another to develop the galaxy's bulge. This theory can also be applied to other similar galaxies, helping us understand their development and the process of galaxy cluster formation.

On November 7, 2004, two massive solar eruptions occurred near the sun's pole.  As these events unfolded along different magnetic field orientations—specifically along north-south lines close to 90 degrees to the earth—they gave rise to five significant solar proton events categorized as M5.5, C7.5, X1.0, X0.5, and X0.5.  Studies have classified these eruptions as poleward solar eruptions that produced high levels of solar radiation.

This research examines how a planet's orbit can become significantly elongated after it interacts with a disk of debris. To understand this phenomenon, we analyzed data from rotating systems involving stars and disks. We found that in some cases, the star and disk are spinning at comparable speeds to each other. However, in other cases, particularly around young stellar objects, the inner part of the system is rotating much faster than expected. To further investigate this discrepancy, we studied theoretical models of spinning material that have been reported in observations. These models suggest that the excess rotation could be caused by the planet having swallowed the entire system. We tested this hypothesis by conducting simulations using a high-resolution code to simulate the interaction between a planet and a disk. If this code had the correct physics to accurately represent the excess rotation, it would have been unable to do so. Consequently, we propose that the unusual rotation speeds observed in some systems may not be evidence of hidden planets, but rather an unanticipated angular momentum transfer between the star and the disk.

The rapid proliferation of news on social media has made it crucial to filter out false information promptly. Despite the engaging content and wide reach of fake news, its false nature is often easy to detect due to structural anomalies. This paper explores the potential for a computer to automatically identify fake news without human intervention, leveraging an innovative network called a Meta Neural Process Network (MNPN). By training this model on diverse datasets containing false and accurate news, it has shown that MNPN can effectively distinguish between the two, even when presented with new content from unknown sources. Furthermore, MNPN excels at identifying previously unrecognized false news originating from sources that the model had not encountered before.

This research report focuses on a convection equation that includes a periodic外力 influence. By applying bifurcation theory, we investigated how initial conditions and periodic外力 can lead to anomalous behavior in a specific model without transformation. Bifurcation analysis reveals that certain semiperiodic solutions can arise from point-like initial data through self-explanatory anomalous behavior.

This paper explores various constructions of Golay complementary sequences (GCS) and sets (GCSets) within the polyphase domain. Notably, new GCSets structures are presented, including an expanded table compiling all known constructions. GCSets have found practical applications in radar signal processing and wireless access code design. Moreover, generalizable formulas for specific sequence pairs, previously established by Tauman and Wang & Yang, are proven in the statistical context.

Silicon's specific crystal structure results in inherent anisotropy within certain electron energy states, which is considered beneficial for quantum computing applications due to inherent directionality. To leverage this attribute, researchers are investigating the ability to control valley interaction between electrons in silicon materials. This study describes several experiments conducted with a scanning tunneling microscope in silicon moesiacs to investigate valley interaction and utilize the intrinsic anisotropy for spin transfer between atoms. By utilizing biexciton states to induce inter-valley exchange interaction and utilize the heavy-hole to light-hole matrix element to transfer spin information. Notably, researchers observed that valley interaction can be utilized to identify the spin of neutral atoms and that intrinsic anisotropy can be employed for efficient spin transfer between silicon atoms.

Graph neural networks have effectively handled various classification and regression tasks within complex systems. Our recent findings provide an in-depth framework, breaking down the dynamics and applications of GNNs in diverse classifications and complex structures. Our framework systematically explores the underlying dynamics of simple and intricate graph structures, ranging from fully connected to highly fragmented configurations. We investigate the source of the predictive capabilities of different graph neural network frameworks, primarily focusing on message passing mechanisms in moderately complex structures. We discovered that successful prediction is tied to the preservation of local information, enabling the propagation of meaningful data within the graph. Our research further examines the limitations of current graph neural network models in highly interconnected systems.

This research paper presents an algorithmic approach to calculating the number of distinct ways two lists of integers can be arranged such that no two adjacent numbers share a common factor. We examine various scenarios derived from homotopy theory, including a method for determining the number of ways the trivial group can be expressed as the product of $n$ factors within a specified group $G$, as well as the number of sequences of $n$ spaces in Group-like homotopy type that have an empty product. Through specific examples, we provide computed results for calculating the number of such arrangements in $n=3,4$ instances for various groups and stable product divisions arising from $n=3,4$ copies of the sphere spectrum.

Understanding how cerebral lesions develop is crucial for advancing knowledge in the field. In this work, we aim to automate this process by generating realistic scissure-type cerebral lesions superimposed on healthy images. Our innovative technique, known as Progressive LAVAE, builds on a prior method called LAVAE, which utilizes two opposing networks to generate lesions with real depth and 2D shading effects. What sets our method apart is the incorporation of a progressive decoding mechanism, enabling realistic lesion images to be generated with greater accuracy. In comparison to the LAVAE baseline, our model produces more accurate and distinguishable cerebral lesions images in terms of both quantitative and qualitative assessments. In addition, our method demonstrates its versatility by generating lesions with varying sizes, depths and shapes on images from different datasets.

GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for high-performance computing, whose compiler transforms source code into a graph format suitable for GP processing. Originally, GP handled graph format data directly, but to improve performance, a compiler is necessary to convert GP instructions into the graph format efficiently. However, the basic CDH compiler lacked sufficient functionality to handle complex programs, necessitating the development of an advanced version. This paper describes the concepts and implementation of a refined GP compiler, known as the enhanced GP compiler, which is realised using Python and integrated as a graph for GP execution.

Recently, feature extraction methods have seen significant advancements with techniques such as autoencoders and contrastive learning gaining popularity. This work introduces a Contrastive Learning Based Feature Extraction (CLAFE) framework that builds upon the Contrastive Learning (ConL) approach. We enhance the ConL approach in three key areas. First, we develop a more comprehensive graph to better represent data relationships. Second, we refine the loss function with a more meaningful distance metric that considers the intrinsic nature of data. Third, we apply the framework in two distinct scenarios: a standard setting and a semi-supervised setting. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed structure, showing superior performance over existing state-of-the-art methods in both settings.

We extend the creation of twisted wreath HNPQDs through a family of groups, denoted as G_k^#, for any positive integer k greater than or equal to 2. These groups are defined as the semidirect products of PSL_2(q^k}) and its corresponding field, q to the power of k, with a cyclic group of order k to the power of 1. For any prime power q greater than or equal to 2, we provide an explicit construction of twisted wreath HNPQDs, associated with PSL_2(q^k}), and offer a comprehensive analysis of their connected components.

Working with categorical data that is high-dimensional and has sparsity patterns becomes significantly more challenging when the categories are non-ordinal, as traditional methods struggle to effectively process such data. This paper introduces an extension of the Group Lasso penalty method, tailored for generalized linear models with categorical responses and covariates. Instead of applying penalties to individual coefficients within each group of categories, the proposed penalty operator acts on the entire group, resulting in the elimination of entire groups of covariates while retaining the entire spectrum of categories within the remaining groups. We utilize the polytomous logit model as an example to demonstrate the applicability of this approach. A gradient-based algorithm is proposed to maximize model performance, and theoretical guarantees regarding model consistency are established. Furthermore, numerical simulations and real-world data analysis show that this method outperforms alternative models in terms of prediction accuracy.

Advancing in LLM capabilities without human intervention leads to hallucinations and inconsistent reasoning. To address these issues, Expert Knowledge Augmentation combines structured knowledge with domain specialists to help training. While effective for smaller models, its benefits diminish for larger models due to information redundancy. Our research introduces the ABILITY framework, which refines knowledge integration by filtering out existing embeddings within the language space. This innovative approach converts knowledge concepts into vector representations and training data into knowledge concepts, using an attention mechanism to calculate conceptual distances and select the most relevant embeddings. The framework relies on a carefully constructed training dataset called Concept-Instruction-Pairs. Our results show that this method significantly enhances performance across various tasks including classification, natural language understanding, and mathematical problem-solving. Specifically, our model achieves a 1.5 to 3.5 percentage point improvement on NLI tasks and a 2.8 times reduction in errors on mathematically related datasets.

A key issue in presenting vector maps on pixel displays is that the lines where paths intersect or connect can experience anti-alignment, causing them to appear broken or misaligned. This issue is particularly prevalent and noticeable at places where paths cross, T-junctions, and L-junctions meet. Although various rendering techniques exist, the position and width of lines are typically fixed, making it difficult to address this issue effectively. In this paper, we introduce an innovative spatial anti-alising method that adjusts line widths in real-time based on their orientation relative to the pixel grid to enhance the visual presentation. We present three innovative solutions - the Variable Width T-Junction Renderer, the Variable Width L-Junction Renderer, and the Variable Width Crossing Renderer - that adapt line widths dynamically. We also propose a general framework for implementing these solutions. Unlike existing methods, our framework and solutions fully address the anti-alising issue at these junctions and crossings, resulting in more seamless and visually appealing presentations of vector maps on pixel displays. Our framework and renderer provide a high-level solution that can be easily integrated into various presenting platforms for vector maps.

To enhance the computation efficiency and modeling capabilities of our previously developed Dual-Path Convolutional Neural Network for speech separation, we've introduced a novel Dual-Path Convolutional Neural Network for Speech Enhancement that utilizes only valid audio samples from a single microphone. Unlike typical approaches, this model can incorporate both time-varying features and external conditions like spatial information into its encoder, while significantly reducing the dimensionality of these inputs in the feed-forward network, allowing us to retain the use of bi-directional LSTM modules without incurring excessive latency. Moreover, we've employed a novel, speech-space invariant prior based on Gaussian processes that enhances generalization capabilities and robustness to varying spatial conditions. Experimental evaluations using both synthetic and real-world data have demonstrated the benefit of incorporating dual pathways, the utilization of spatial priors and modulations, and the model achieves superior performance when compared to current state-of-the-art methods.

To advance atmospheric convection modeling efficiency, we plan to develop a multi-fluid approach using cloud-resolving models. Before venturing into complex multi-fluid simulations with numerous atmospheric constituents, a two-fluid case is intended to be simulated on a single column. This simulation will incorporate the effects of diffusion and phase change in both dry and moist air. By leveraging the existing atmospheric convection equation framework, we anticipate significantly accelerating our modeling process. The research starts by validating numerical methods with analytical solutions to known problems. subsequently, two-fluid simulations are presented for both dry and moist conditions. These simulations demonstrate the model's capability to capture convection, phase change, and cloud formation accurately. Nonetheless, there are challenges with phase boundary resolution that require further investigation. Overall, this research establishes the feasibility of a two-fluid single-column model and provides the foundation for an efficient multi-fluid atmospheric convection model.

In this study, we investigate the dynamics of two independent Jaynes-Cummings interfaces involving qubit-assemblages. Assuming the initial states of the interfaces are either product states or maximally entangled, we demonstrate that the non-markovian time evolution gives rise to entanglement between the interfaces, even in the absence of direct interaction. We further prove that this generated entanglement is strongly resistant to decoherence, resulting in marksovian dynamics that exhibit stable, small-amplitude oscillations in certain regimes. Our findings indicate that the JC-induced entanglement is fundamentally distinct from that generated via common-mode dynamics.

Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them or other subjects.
Traditional methods for assessing sentiment on social media inputs rely on large annotated
datasets, expert-created rules, or classification models based on external datasets.
This study explores the use of unsupervised methods to generate sentiment scores for
Textual data, utilizing a neural network architecture that allows for score differentiation
between consecutive time periods.
An approach is proposed that combines unsupervised ranking techniques with an LSTM
framework to assess the sentiment of public communications.
The effectiveness of this model is validated using the Nanagani et al. (2017) dataset,
showing that it produces more accurate results than conventional unsupervised methods for
determining the sentiment of public communications.

A nonlinear interaction between scalar fields and electromagnetism can lead to a new type of black hole in an anti-de Sitter space, and this paper explores how this interaction influences the behavior of shadow images and the Page curve of extremal black holes. By calculating the impact of these nonlinear parameters on the shape of shadow images and the geometry of the photon sphere, we find that they play significant roles in determining the black hole's properties. Notably, the nonlinear parameters can cause the shadow images of rotating black holes to break their usual symmetry, and can also result in the extremal Page curve without semi-classical effects. Furthermore, we discuss how these findings can be used to detect and understand these parameters experimentally.

Recent experiments on macroscopic objects have identified a brief period of quantum entanglement and the onset of emerging correlations immediately following a measurement instance. A Tomogram-based formalism has been employed to quantify these phenomena, demonstrating that the onset of correlations can be detected when the Wigner function is positive-definite. Conversely, actual entanglement formation was found to require a preceding period of non-Gaussian correlations, as evidenced by deviations in the shape of the probability distribution. A theoretical model illustrating this process has been applied to explain the recent experiment conducted by "The entanglement of identical macroscopic objects", as well as it reveals a brief period of entanglement during the initial stages of divergence in identical macroscopic objects evolving according to a Schrödinger's cat-like scenario.

360-degree video travel experiences often suffer from user navigation errors, 
which can be mitigated by forecasting user viewpoints.  A dataset named VT360 and a 
baseline forecast model are provided in this paper, upon which captions for video 
frames are utilized to predict user viewpoints.  Experimental results indicate that 
users are most likely to look in a specific direction in given situations, e.g., 
when watching an ship, there's a high probability that they will look to its side. 
However, forecasting models struggle to accurately predict user gaze directions, 
which may be due to the inherent symmetry in many scenes and the limited information 
contained in video frames.

We investigate tensor network methods for modeling pure thermal states and temporal dynamics in two-dimensional conformal field theories (CFTs). Our state construction technique, based on local operations and classical communication (LOCC), allows us to calculate thermodynamic properties and correlation functions, while preserving precise spatial entanglement structure. Our approach yields the correct entropy scaling on a spatial interval as temperature increases from infinite to near zero, and similarly, it results in the correct scaling of time-evolution entropy after a quench. Our tensor network model accurately replicates HPTE scaling in both thermal and time-evolution scenarios.

We develop a decoupling theory that approximates the cardinality of any cardinality-restricted copy of a variety. Specifically, for a variety $V$ in $\mathbb{F}_p^n$, when a cardinality-restricted copy $V'$ of $V$ has a limited number of solutions, we find that it can be represented as the union of $v v^{4/n} p^{2/3}/\log ^{2}p$ copies of low variance surfaces, where each copy is positioned at a point where $V$ exhibits minimal curvature, and the cardinality of $V'$ at any location is limited. This result is utilized to demonstrate that most copies of $V$ with a limited number of solutions are closely aligned with one location or can be described as the union of some variety of highly curved copies of $V$ with significantly reduced cardinalities. These findings are applicable to a range of decoupling and restriction theory problems.

The research investigates the error margins of the nucleon color dipole operator within the high-energy range, which is a key element in the nonlinear evolution of Gluon TMD PDF, particularly as it pertains to the nucleon at a small x value. Calculated at leading and next-to-leading orders, the radius of the infrared renormalon cone is found to be approximately 0.5 GeV, which is consistent with observed color dipole sizes from global data fits (around 0.45-0.5 GeV). Furthermore, an estimate of the associated uncertainty is made, which influences the xg(x) behavior as it occurs in the small x regime.

The development of high-dimensional lattice structures is driving innovation in lattice optics and physics, prompting exploration of higher-dimensional phenomena such as photonic quasicrystals and topological lattices. However, traditional diffraction limitations and complex fabrication lattice methods restrict the creation of high-dimensional lattices, restricting researchers to lower-dimensional structures. This project focuses on devising a compact and efficient two-step holographic method to create the lattice pattern directly on chip-scale devices using UV photolithography. This method combines the desired lattice structure with a binary phase grating that orients the lattice orientation based on light propagation direction. As a result, the created device can generate distinct interference patterns when light is shone at it in different directions. The device was validated through rigorous computer simulations and experimental experiments, demonstrating the holographic approach's feasibility and effectiveness.

Decision outcomes framework, formulated by Apple, is a black-box structure that processes decisions based on an underlying, unaccessible model. This framework is highly beneficial in processing vast data streams in real-time. Our decision outcomes framework relies on a decision model, which can be trained using transfer learning to take advantage of existing models. Transfer learning can significantly reduce the requirement for new data and computational resources when model updates are necessary. In the context of transfer learning, zero-shot knowledge transfer stands out as it employs an unrelated target model without fine-tuning, thereby minimizing data leakage risks. Our investigation into this zero-shot knowledge transfer approach reveals its effectiveness, showing performance gains of up to 35% compared to starting from scratch. Our results also provide decision model transfer learning recommendations.

Researchers have observed the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_L$ decay mode for the first time, and have also gathered evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_L$ decay mode, utilizing a 3.0 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ dataset of $pp$ collisions collected at 7 and 8 TeV center-of-mass energies by the LHCb. The branching fractions for these decays are calculated as follows: The $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_L$ branching fraction is estimated at (4.3$^{+1.4}_{-1.3}\text{(stat)}\pm 0.2\text{(sys)}\ ) \times 10^{-4},$ while the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_L$ branching fraction is estimated at (1.9$^{+0.6}_{-0.5}\text{(stat)}\pm 0.1\text{(sys)}\ ) \times 10^{-4}.

Given a reductive group $G$ over the complex numbers, there is a lattice of submodules beneath $a$ distinguished Borel subgroup $B$, with its elements corresponding to intermediate modules between $B$ and $G$. By restricting to the set of atoms and coatoms within this lattice, its structural properties can be determined based on the geometric characteristics of certain arrangements of hyperplanes. Specifically, the atoms correspond to submodules whose defining subgroups are related to the maximal torus in $G$, while the coatoms are associated with maximal solvable subgroups of $G$. This method is applicable to all reductive groups, including those of type $E_8$, and is built upon foundational concepts established by Severi and Chevalley.

This study investigates a new multi-agent learning scenario called co-observation learning, where multiple agents operate within the same Markov decision process but have access to partially combined observations of the same state and actions of all other agents are visible to all. We expand our initial formulation to accommodate a broader range of applications by refining state and action visibility. In contrast to learning from scratch, we develop policy transfer approaches that enable agents with new IDs to benefit from the knowledge of others. Our results include transfer-based algorithms for fully observable settings, yielding near-optimal sample efficiency with a theoretical bound of $\tilde{O}((SA)^{2/3}\sqrt{SHAPC})$, where $\tilde{O}$ hides polynomial factors of $S$, $A$, and $P$, and we demonstrate that this can be improved to $\tilde{O}(SA\sqrt{HPC})$ for tabular cases, with $P$ denoting the number of players and $C$ the number of cooperative agents. Furthermore, our research highlights the significance of learning in a setting with changing rewards, leading to an FPAUC performance metric and associated theoretical guarantees.

This paper fills in metrics related to PAC codes and establishes their relationship to Guava's code distance function. We demonstrate that the distance between zero and a specific code c is equivalent to the weight of c, and also provide a metric for determining the distance between two codes. Furthermore, we provide step-by-step calculations of the distances between the PAC codes and the code representing the English language.

We investigate the use of reinforcement learning techniques for enhancing the performance of neural machine translation models, focusing on reducing translation errors measured by BLEU metrics. To achieve this, we developed two unconventional, high-cost action spaces for refining model predictions: an exploration space, which involves selectively amplifying and shifting token probabilities to introduce variability, and a extraction space, which targets and removing specific parts of the translation to facilitate easier correction. Our findings demonstrate that this framework leads to models that consistently outperform the standard training method, yielding improvements of roughly 0.5 BLEU in multiple scenarios.

Weexaminees both empirically and computationally the non-equilibrium steady state of a quantum bit subjected to periodic driving forces. 
Our findings demonstrate that the dynamics of the quantum bit's phase space can be traced back to three distinct behaviors: stable oscillations, growing exponential patterns, and persistent non-simplistic designs. Additionally, we observed that when certain conditions are met, even minute measurements can significantly influence the amplitude of pre-existing exponential patterns. 
Our findings also highlight that by observing a quantum bit under specific conditions, we can rapidly distinguish between theoretical predictions and actual performance, allowing for efficient error correction strategies.

This study classifies biharmonic hypersurfaces within Euclidean spacetimes, satisfying a set of conditions where both Laplacians, applied consecutively, yield the zero outcome from a rank-2 matrix, referred to as having a repetitive operator structure. Our investigation delves into the characteristics of these hypersurfaces, ultimately discovering their intrinsic semi-umbilical nature following the application of a single operator. Ultimately, we establish their explicit form as the Cartesian product of the spherical hypersurface and the Euclidean cylinder following the removal of its closed part. Conversely, when assuming an initial intrinsic umbilical property following a single operator application, we define their corresponding form as either a spherical hypersurface or its product with the Euclidean cylinder, again excluding its closed component.

A set of strings is called $p/q$-identifiable from observations $p/q$-distinct from each other if a probabilistic algorithm can accurately determine whether it belongs to the set based on a single, unique sample from the set, but is unable to do so without a specific ratio of additional samples to classification errors that decreases as the complexity of the task increases given only non-unique distributions. This concept is related to standard identifiability and mutual identifiability, but differs in its treatment of the relationship between the complexity of the task and the complexity of the classifier.

MongoDB is a widely used NoSQL database known for its flexibility and performance in diverse applications. However, its initial version lacked robust support for strict transactional integrity. This paper aims to verify and illustrate MongoDB's transactional capabilities across its various data engines: WiredTiger, MMAPv1, and InnoDB. Through in-depth unit testing and custom failure simulation frameworks, our studies confirmed that all three engines guarantee transactional accuracy during normal operations and when faced with sudden system failures. Our findings demonstrate that MongoDB's transactions adhere to the ACID (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability) principle, ensuring reliable data management.

We demonstrate that a specific statistic, measured on the combinatorial structures known as colored permutations, accounts for $e_m n! h_n$ where colored permutations are defined and studied here. This category of objects was initially established by Huh and the concept of $e$-positivity here is applied to provide an alternative proof for the $e$-positivity of the chromatic symmetric monomial functions, denated as $\sigma_n$, as per the work of MacPherson and Stanley. Moreover, we provide a combinatorial explanation for the $e$-positivity of $\omega A_n$ through the use of a set of combinatorial objects called signed colored permutations.

Research on intricate networks has uncovered hidden geometric principles that significantly impact intricate network dynamics. To expose this concealed geometry and its impact on intricate network dynamics, researchers have developed a novel algorithm to translate intricate magnetic material interactions into a geometric graph framework. When applied to a nanoscale triangular lattice with both pairwise and triangular interactions, this framework reveals that intricate network dynamics are governed by the intricate geometry and spin frustration within specific sub-geometric clusters. Furthermore, the intricate geometry and spin frustration within these clusters can lead to a phenomenon known as the concealment of triple-Herringbone (trh) configurations, resulting in an abrupt and enigmatic collective spin behavior.

The inner heliosphere is an ideal location for studying the interaction of the sun with the interstellar medium, as well as investigating solar breeze energy mechanisms. The newly launched Parker Solar Probe, now gathering data, is designed to collect detailed information in the inner solar system and is set to approach as close as 9.76 solar radii in subsequent missions. The probe's instruments, including the Plasma Spectrometer (PASI), are set to measure close-up electron and ion populations in the solar breeze, as well as their temperatures, precursors, and energy transmission methods. The initial data from the first three encounters of the PSP with the inner solar system reveals the prevalence of protons and the diversity of solar breeze ion populations, allowing researchers to assess electron population energy transmission. The first analysis of PSP data aims to establish baseline energy statistics in the inner heliosphere and sets the stage for long-term studies of the interstellar interaction. The results of such an investigation may include updates to the solar system's mass, momentum, and energy flux estimates, as well as corrections to historical assumptions underlying the Interstellar Boundary Exploration predictions of the local interstellar medium near the Earth.

This paper explores our progress and techniques in adapting speech-emotion recognition models across various domains, with a focus on using self-supervised methods and adapting to new domains without labeled data. We discuss the challenges and potential solutions in this field, including adapting pre-trained models to new domains with limited or no labeled labels, the difficulties of speech-emotion recognition, and the potential for domain adaptation techniques to improve these models. Overall, this article serves as a guide to the potential applications and limitations of domain adaptation in speech-emotion recognition.

This study investigates a newly discovered situation within an adiabatically and uniformly expanding cosmic environment, specifically comparing two models: one with a solitary spherical void and another filled with matter. We find that during a particular intermediate phase, the剧烈 shock wave generated by the collapse of the void's inner wall becomes infinitely intense, marking a theoretical limit of hydrodynamics. Our findings are illustrated through numerical simulations, revealing the intense pressure generated by the shock wave's stagnation point could give rise to the formation of stars or galaxies.

Using a collection of $364\,\,\,\rm pb$ of $\rm LEP$ data, researchers from both CERN and the University of Birmingham studied $D_s^{*-}$$\,\,\mu^{+}\,\,\,\nu_{\mu}$ final states originating from $B_s^0\,\rightarrow\,\,D_s^{*-}\,\,\,\mu^{+}\,\,\,\nu_{\mu}$ decays to determine the behavior of these decays without relying on theoretical predictions. By focusing on these decays and utilizing a maximum likelihood method, they were able to directly visualize the form of the differential decay rate. They found that the differential decay rate is composed of three components, each corresponding to the $D_s^{*-}$'s polarization states, with significant constraints placed on the corresponding form factors at a confidence level of $950$. Additionally, they were able to set new, tighter confidence intervals for the differences in $B_s^0$ and $D_s^{*-}$ masses with a confidence level of $95$.

A detailed examination of the one-dimensional Schrödinger-Courant system reveals an algebraic method for constructing its solutions. This involves using special polynomials that generalize the classical Hermite polynomials. These polynomials serve as building blocks for constructing solutions with specific properties at certain points. Furthermore, researchers have identified their corresponding potential functions and identified their quantum states. A further exploration of linear Schrödinger-Courant equations has led to defining point-separating polynomials that expand upon traditional polynomial solutions. This in turn has resulted in defining a specialized class of polynomial SCN systems and defining their associated generalized Hermite polynomials, which also include defining their corresponding potential functions and quantum states.

Recent advances in research have explored acoustic signatures resulting from stress failures in materials, an area that the current study builds upon, an investigation into the acoustic emissions produced when polyethylene tape peels off a metal surface. A significant discovery was made during the study of the tape's unrolling process on aluminum alloy, acoustic activity associated with a specific resonance frequency of approximately 2.2 kHz. This activity diminishes during transitions between the tape's stick and slip phases but absent in vacuum conditions or when tape with altered thickness is used. As a result, a substantial amount of information is compiled that may serve the basis for a new stress failure model that considers macroscopic stress contributors.

We perform a thermodynamic analysis of the non-abelian ether-like term with density and temperature dependencies, denoted as $\bar{\theta}\int dt d^3x \frac{1}{a^3(t)}{\rm Tr}(\mathcal{F}_{\mu\nu}\tilde{\mathcal{F}}^{\mu\nu})$. As the temperature increases, we observe a non-abelian phase transition occurring within the SU(N) gauge theory. Furthermore, we investigate the non-abelian ether-like term's impact on the behavior of gluons and axions in an expanding universe. Our theoretical predictions, particularly concerning jet suppression and the spectrum of cosmic microwave background radiation, could provide evidence for the non-abelian ether-like term after observational confirmation of cosmic inflation. We also discover that the non-abelian ether-like term leads to a non-trivial drag force, axial charge generation, and modifications in the diffusion term within a quark-gluum plasma, as well as the $\bar{\theta}$-induced dipole meson's altered dispersion relation.

This research examines the pricing and hedging of options on options, highlighting the necessity of calculating dynamic delta-hedging costs and exploring the impact of collateral agreements on pricing options options. As prices of underlying options result from applying a heat equation, initially proposed by Leippold and Prigent, we develop a analytical formula for expected future hedging costs, allowing for various collateral agreements and option futures. Our model incorporates non-linear time-volatility and time-dependent heat equation to create an extensive and flexible framework for research. This research opens up new avenues of investigation into expected future hedging costs, including various sources of risk premiums, the impact of option options on pricing European options, and potential applications in financial derivatives.

A dynamic general equilibrium model demonstrates how intergenerational mobility limitations affect opportunities distribution across economic activities, leading to dominant sectors with large concentrations of professionals and numerous marginal ones. The model's assumptions also result across generations sticky sectors, explaining economic development's lack of diversity. We further show that policies or shocks enhancing marginal sector diversity can create new, self-sustaining economic opportunities.

This study investigates the benefits and limitations of using brightness scans to analyze particle beams. Although initially developed for full beam analysis, this technique can also be applied to partial beam scans to determine beam parameters. This study establishes the relationship between full and partial scans through an integral that allows for the extraction of partial scan parameters, provided certain conditions are met. For cases where these conditions are not fulfilled, corrections can be implemented. Furthermore, for beams with uniform profiles, brightness scans offer an efficient means of determining the shape of the profile without extensive measurements, as well as for monitoring beams with evolving profiles. This study also investigates the limitations of using brightness scans to analyze slow beams, demonstrating that they can reveal local properties of such beams rather than a comprehensive picture.

This paper explores an optimized algorithm for multi-agent systems through the use of a distributed optimization method that avoids the need for agents to exchange heavily sized data. The proposed method achieves the same results as the optimized algorithm through the use of rounded numerical values in a networked environment. The method is applicable in various fields including signal processing, telecommunications and machine learning.

To enhance the accuracy of cosmological models derived from Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) data, it is crucial to analyze and understand the instrument-related systematic errors. This paper presents a method for incorporating real instrumental systematic errors into Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) analyses at the observation level. Our algorithm efficiently integrates the measured data, theoretical forecasts, and instrumental systematic uncertainties into the likelihood calculation by precalculating measurement operators for each frequency channel. This MCMC-compatible technique has been realized in the s4cmb software package. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, we applied it to simulate the systematic errors associated with temperature polarization converters (TPCs) and demonstrated their impact on MCMC analyses using the s4cmb package. Our findings revealed that failing to consider these instrumental systematic errors could adversely affect the derived cosmological parameters, thereby emphasizing the significance of accurately modeling and analyzing such errors to improve the reliability of CMB data-derived cosmological models.

In our research, we discovered that pre-trained language models, specifically BART, fulfill a restoration function in word sequence completion tasks. Our analysis built upon a solid foundation involving synthetic datasets and linguistic theory, highlighting how BART's capacity to restore disrupted sentences is intimately connected to its understanding of natural language. Our findings are further validated through experiments with multiple state-of-the-art natural language understanding models, establishing that the restoration function is a key component of the representations learned by these models. Furthermore, we established a direct relationship between a model's natural language understanding capabilities and its performance on various tasks, including natural language inference, paragraph reasoning, and the recently introduced Wikipedia shuffling benchmark. To enhance performance, we devised a novel framework for paragraph reasoning that achieved state-of-the-art results, surpassing previous records set by these models.

The rapid dissemination of ultra-realistic multimedia content on multiple social media platforms necessitates the development of an efficient and reliable deepfake detection method to prevent misinformation and deception. Existing deepfake detection techniques suffer from poor generalization能力 due to biased training data across different social media environments. In this study, we propose a novel single-model deepfake detection framework called the MD-CSDNetwork, which incorporates a novel detection head and utilizes cross-domain knowledge to distinguish fake samples from real ones across various domains without requiring labeled data. Experimental results using several well-known deepfake datasets confirm the effectiveness of our approach, demonstrating improved performance compared to the state-of-the-art methods.

In 1930, mathematician K. Menger developed a comprehensive framework for representing geometric figures in abstract space. Within this framework, he identified limitations concerning the definition of angles, finding that it required additional, unrelated, properties to function effectively. Menger proposed three potential approaches and questions regarding how angles could be described within this abstract framework. Recent research by Abrahamsen and Soler-Peris confirms that all but one of Menger's approaches can be characterized specifically, providing a solution to his initial query about defining angles in linear geometries.

A central area of algebraic number theory investigates the properties of lattice sequences within number fields. These lattice sequences are intimately connected to various concepts, such as ideal classes in number fields, fractional ideals, and the ring of integers. A key objective in this area of research is the establishment of inequalities governing the product of successive minima of lattices. This report reviews recent advancements in this field, with a focus on my own contributions, and derives formulas to estimate the ratio of successive minima of the ring of integers in a number field. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of these inequalities by utilizing them to resolve an open question posed by Silverman regarding the ratio of minima of fields defined by the root of a quadratic polynomial over finite fields, as well as a class of cubic and quartic extensions of $\mathbb{Q}$. In each instance, the ratio of minima is shown to be equal to N(\mathfrak{f})^{1/2}, N(\mathfrak{f}), or \frac{2}{3}N(\mathfrak{f})^{\frac{4}{3}}, where N(\mathfrak{f}) denotes the product of the norms of the radical of the ring of integers.

Using a cluster algebra framework, we establish the Fock-Vershik representation of the quantum group $U_q(\widehat{\mathfrak{sl}}_2)$ at the level of the space of vertex operator representations. This finding builds upon earlier work by Geer-Ruiz and Le-Moizey for non-primeness level $p \geq 5$. Furthermore, we observe the inapplicability of our result at the level $p=3$. Moreover, we apply and extend a result from Berenstein-Sassoon regarding the cluster nature of the affine Lie algebra at the level three, incorporating input from Le's work on the three-fold tensor property at level three.

Pyramid schemes, long condemned in traditional banking and finance, have recently shifted to blockchain technology. We analyze the Forsage, a particularly egregious example of a pyramid scheme built into a decentralized application. Our study aims to better understand how pyramid schemes operate within blockchain networks and highlights the structural differences between traditional and digital versions of these schemes. We break down the Forsage scheme's complex pricing mechanisms and examine the risks for both early adopters and latecomers. Our research also provides law enforcement and regulatory authorities with valuable insights into tracking and prosecuting digital pyramid schemes.

In this study, we identify potential new globular cluster candidates in the VVV survey data spanning the Galactic bulge using color-magnitude diagrams. Our initial findings highlight at least eleven previously unrecorded clusters: NBSS 90,91,92,93,94,95,96,97,98,99, and 100. These clusters span a total area of 40 square degrees. NBSS 090 and 091 were found in the Scutum-1 bar, whereas the remaining nine were discovered in the Sagittarius arm. Spectroscopic analysis of field stars near these clusters reveals they share the same metallicity as surrounding areas. However, we found that two of them, NBSS 092 and 093, exhibit distinct lower levels of abundance compared to their neighbors and the VVV sample. Consequently, they may be classified as new globular clusters. Their characteristics suggest they likely formed in the Sagittarius starforming complex. Their formation timing could be either recent in the last few billion years or corresponding to the era of the galaxy's thick disk. Their small masses and lack of recorded asteroseismic variables suggest they may be among the first clusters discovered in this region.

In the context of critical systems, where local interactions lead to power-law correlations, tensor network models like MERA are used to efficiently represent the system's ground state. A key challenge in these models is accurately simulating the time-evolution of the many-body system, particularly due to the spatial expansion of the geodesic in the tensor network. Our research introduces a novel component for the MERA model, called the hyper-link, which is placed between adjacent sites of the tensor and can efficiently simulate local Hamiltonian dynamics. This new model, called hyper-MERA, is found to geometrically represent the system's state and effectively function as a holographic quantum error correcting code. Geometrically, we found that hyper-MERA models and Hamiltonian dynamics can be thought of as being inscribed within a hyper-sphere. Furthermore, our study reveals that the hyper-link tensor provides a direct correlation between the base of the tensor network and the quantum states of the system, allowing for an in-depth analysis of entanglement entropy and correlation lengths. We also found that the hyper-link tensor plays a crucial role in determining the behavior of these correlations and entropy, similar to the role of the diagonal tensor. Finally, our model is proposed as a reliable starting point for numerical simulations of 1D critical systems using MERA models.

The rapid expansion of industrial scales and technological advancements have fueled the growth of large datasets, leading to the emergence of various machine learning and deep learning methods for identifying patterns and making predictions in complex processes. In the specific context of business process management, numerous studies have been conducted using deep learning and hybrid machine learning techniques for both understanding and predicting workflows. To further delve into this subject, this study examines deep learning and hybrid approaches for both understanding the underlying structure of business processes and predicting their dependent variables. In addition to deep learning studies, a comparison is made with traditional machine learning methods for the same business processes. The studies being compared include utilizing neural networks and ensemble algorithms such as random forests and gradient boosting models. To facilitate a comprehensive understanding, visualizations of the dependency structure of business processes are generated using graph-based representations. Furthermore, predictive accuracy is evaluated using regression and classification models to predict the dependent variables of the business processes. Ultimately, the results obtained from deep learning and ensemble algorithms are discussed in detail.

We investigate key properties of several character areas, specifically Gelfand-Shilov areas, and establish their non-triviality. To do this, we provide characterization methods for these areas, particularly through the use of the Fourier transform. These areas, first defined by Canzani and Sogge, are essential in determining decay rates of solutions to partial differential equations. We obtain non-triviality results for K-symmetric functions and those with polynomial growth under certain conditions, including when applied to the symbol of a Toeplitz operator on the complex plane. To establish our findings, we characterize the surjectivity of the Fourier transform on Gelfand-Shilov spaces, which allows us to determine conditions under which the Fourier transform of a function remains within the same class. We also extend previous results and offer a new approach to proving non-triviality of the Gelfand-Shilov area.

A stellar flare occurrence, particularly of huge magnitude like a HET, poses significant challenges in modeling the spectral energy distribution (SED) during such events. The intensity and broad scope of energy from HET flares can outshine the stellar material, leading to difficulties in analyzing and understanding the underlying physical processes leading up to such eruptions. Ad Leo, a known X-ray and UV flare star, had its most massive eruption recorded in 1985 during its outburst, providing an extensive dataset for a detailed UV spectral energy model. Using the UV data from multiple sources, an comprehensive UV spectrum model of the 1985 April 12 great eruption of Ad Leo was created. Analyzing the UV spectrum during this great event revealed three major components contributing to the overall flux: the UV interstellar absorption, stellar hydrogen and helium line emissions, and UV continuum. Based on theoretical modeling, the UV continuum resulted from high-energy particles interacting with the stellar material, leading to extensive surface heating and electron beam-induced emission (CXRRE). The UV spectrum model of the 1985 April 12 great eruption of Ad Leo offers an essential foundation for further research into HET flare physical processes.

Lidar sensors lack reliability in adverse weather conditions like rain, snow, and fog, leading to noisy and distorted point cloud images that hinder the performance of subsequent processing steps. A challenging task is to filter out these outliers while avoiding the removal of fragments. Existing methods have limitations, including a high risk of over-smoothing and under-smoothing, as well as issues with real-time processing. To address this, a novel approach called TPC (Transformation Point Cloud Smoothing) is presented, which utilizes scaling and rotation to fill gaps in data and employs adaptive kernels to fill missing fragments. Furthermore, a compact model is developed to facilitate efficient processing. Experimental results on difficult datasets show that TPC excels in point cloud smoothing performance.

Within the RPA framework and utilizing the jost function method, a study was conducted to highlight the capabilities of this approach in handling intricate RPA responses and determining complex eigenenergies. RPA equations were applied to the electric dipole response of $^{16}$O at a an energy resolution of 0.05 MeV. A complicated eigenenergy in the range of 30-31 MeV was found, along with additional uncomplicated eigenenergies, all derived from fundamental inputs without prior knowledge of final results. When compared to established experimental and theoretical data, the RPA predictions showed a degree of agreement, although they also contained some discrepancies. A uncomplicated RPA eigenenergy in the range of 18 MeV was found to align with the primary RPA peak of $^{16}$O, while the intricate RPA eigenenergy at 30.3 MeV was determined to correspond to it.

We present a novel clustering technique for dynamical systems, integrating linear models like Recurrent Neural Networks (LSTM) and Autoencoders, to identify inherent groupings in complex data sets. Unlike conventional unsupervised methods, our approach leverages pre-trained models, accounting for the intrinsic structure and non-stationary nature of dynamical data. We employ data-driven exploration tools, including covariance analysis and manifold alignment, to cluster high-dimensional data, demonstrating the effectiveness of our technique through various applications and comparisons with standard methods. Our results highlight the utility of this technique for identifying and tracking inherent cluster groupings in time-varying data.

Deep neural technologies have revolutionized text generation, yet they require extensive data with word representations that are both expansive and cumbersome. In this research, we propose a novel approach called the Sparse Generative Antagonistic Network (SGAN) that utilizes a factor analysis-based method to derive sparse textual representations for generation purposes. Our network comprises two key components - a generator and a discriminator, both of which are built around sparse coding principles. In contrast to traditional SGAN models that employ deep neural networks, our approach eschews non-linearity, allowing the SGAN to achieve superior performance on three distinct tasks involving text generation. Our experimental findings demonstrate that the SGAN outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques in the realms of caption writing, style transfer, and translation.

The theory of interstellar panspermia posits that complex organic molecules could be transferred between galaxies, potentially contributing to the diversity of life forms. For this hypothesis to hold, organisms must withstand extreme conditions during their journey, including high-energy radiation and violent cosmic events. In this study, we investigate the effects of such phenomena on protected organisms within meteorites, modeling the radiation they would be exposed to in intergalactic space and during their entry into stellar systems. We also assess the damage caused by violent events like gamma-ray bursts and supernovae. Our analysis suggests that while organisms might suffer significant cellular damage, they could potentially survive and reproduce, given that complex organic structures are highly resilient.
